Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and 
Applications 
The book series Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and Applications (FAIA) covers all aspects of 
theoretical and applied Artificial Intelligence research in the form of monographs, selected 
doctoral dissertations, handbooks and proceedings volumes. The FAIA series contains several 
sub-series, including ‘Information Modelling and Knowledge Bases’ and ‘Knowledge-Based 
Intelligent Engineering Systems’. It also includes the biennial European Conference on Artificial 
Intelligence (ECAI) proceedings volumes, and other EurAI (European Association for Artificial 
Intelligence, formerly ECCAI) sponsored publications. The series has become a highly visible platform for the publication and dissemination of original research in this field. Volumes are 
selected for inclusion by an international editorial board of well-known scholars in the field of 
AI. All contributions to the volumes in the series have been peer reviewed. 
All volumes within the FAIA series are indexed in ACM Digital Library; DBLP; EI Compendex; 
Google Scholar; Scopus; Zentralblatt MATH. All volumes are submitted for individual 
evaluation by Web of Science: Conference Proceedings Citation Index (CPCI).

Foreword 
Interest in technological advances – be that processing, or representation and 
engineering – as they relate to legal information and knowledge, has been growing for 
decades. Formal and computational models of legal reasoning, legal data analytics, legal information retrieval, the application of machine learning techniques to various 
legal tasks, and experimental evaluations of these systems have all been active research 
areas, and seem likely to continue to be so. 
This book presents the proceedings of JURIX 2025, the 38th International 
Conference on Legal Knowledge and Information Systems, held from 9 to 11 December in Turin, Italy, under the auspices of the JURIX Foundation for Legal Knowledge-Based Systems, and hosted by the University of Turin. The annual JURIX 
conference has become an international forum for academics and professionals to 
exchange knowledge and experiences at the intersection of law and artificial intelligence (AI). For this edition, we received 139 eligible submissions (of which 103 
were long papers) by 392 authors from 35 countries. Following a rigorous review 
process, carried out by a programme committee of 107 experts recognised in the field, 22 submissions were selected for publication as long papers and 18 as short papers, 
representing a 21.3% acceptance rate for long papers (per long submissions, 15,8% for 
long papers per all submissions) and 28.7% overall (accepted for presentation/all 
submissions). An additional 18 submissions were accepted as posters. The wide range 
of topics covered includes formal approaches (deontic logic, cased-based reasoning, formal argumentation, and other formalisms) applied to various aspects of legal 
reasoning, machine learning (large language models, including conversational agents) 
and information retrieval methods applied to various natural language processing tasks, hybrid approaches to working on the frontiers between symbolic and sub-symbolic 
methods, experimental inquiries on interfaces between computational systems and legal 
systems, and network analysis in the law. 
Providing an overview of recent advances, the book will be of interest to all those 
working at the intersection of law and AI.  v

Preface JURIX 2025 
We are pleased to present the proceedings of JURIX 2025, the 38th International 
Conference on Legal Knowledge and Information Systems. Organised under  
the auspices of the Foundation for Legal Knowledge-Based Systems (https:// www.jurix.nl), the JURIX annual conference has become established as an 
internationally renowned forum for the exchange of ideas concerning theoretical 
models and practical applications in the broadly construed domain of artificial intelligence (AI) and law research, including legal information systems and legal 
knowledge systems research. Traditionally, the field of AI and law has been concerned 
with legal knowledge representation and engineering, logic, and computational models of legal reasoning, legal data analytics, and legal information retrieval, but recent years 
have witnessed the rise to prominence of the application of machine learning tools to 
legally relevant tasks, recently joined by a sharp increase in the exploitation of large language model (LLM)-based AI agents and systems for law-related tasks. 
Furthermore, the constantly growing influence of AI on different spheres of social life 
has prompted interest in the explainability, trustworthiness, and responsibility of computational systems. From their inception, the JURIX conferences have been a 
venue for interdisciplinary research, integrating methods, approaches, and conceptual 
frameworks from different branches of computer science and jurisprudence, including 
cognitive and socio-technical dimensions.  
The 2025 edition of JURIX, which runs from 9 to 11 December, is hosted by the 
University of Turin, in Turin, Italy. An exponential growth in the number of submissions was experienced for this editi on compared to previous years, with 139 
eligible submissions (of which 103 were long papers) by 392 authors from 35 countries 
being received. Following a rigorous review process, carried out by a programme 
committee of 107 experts recognised in the field, 22 submissions were selected for 
publication as long papers and 18 as short papers, representing a 21.3% acceptance rate for long papers (per long submissions, 15.8% for long papers per all submissions) and 
28.7% overall (accepted for presentation/all submissions). An additional 18 
submissions were accepted as posters. The accepted papers cover a wide range of topics, including formal approaches (deontic logic, case-based reasoning, formal 
argumentation, and other formalisms) applied to various aspects of legal reasoning, 
machine learning, natural language processing and information retrieval methods as applied to various legal tasks, hybrid approaches working on the frontiers between 
symbolic and sub-symbolic methods, experimental enquiries on interfaces between 
computational systems and legal systems, and network analysis in law. 
Two invited speakers, Marie-Francine Moens and Tiago Cabral, have honoured 
JURIX 2025 by kindly agreeing to deliver keynote lectures.  
Marie-Francine Moens pioneered in NLP for AI&Law; we now live in a world 
(partly) shaped by her. She is currently a professor emerita at KU Leuven, Belgium. From 1992 to 2007, she was a researcher, guest professor and associate professor at the Centre for Law and ICT, and later became a professor and full professor at the 
Department of Computer Science at KU Leuven. vi

Marie-Francine Moens received the ERC Advanced Grant CALCULUS (2018-
2024), awarded by the European Research Council. From 2012 to 2016, she was the 
coordinator of the MUSE project financed by Future and Emerging Technologies (FET) of the European Commission. In 2021, she was the general chair of the 2021 
Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2021). In 
2011 and 2012, she was appointed as chair of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (EACL) and was a member of the executive board of 
the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL). She is currently associate editor 
of the journal IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI) and of the journal AI Open. In 2014, she was a Scottish Informatics and 
Computer Science Alliance (SICSA) Distinguished Visiting Fellow. She is a fellow of 
the European Laboratory for Learning and Intelligent Systems (ELLIS). Her research topics include machine learning for natural language processing; representation 
learning for language grounding in the physical and social world; deep learning, latent 
variable models and brain-inspired models; and machine learning models for structured prediction and generation. 
Tiago Sérgio Cabral is a Legal and Policy Officer at the European Commission, 
where he works in the European AI Office in the team responsible for AI Regulation and Compliance. He specializes in Artificial Intelligence, Data Protection, and 
Cybersecurity. He holds a PhD in Legal Sciences – Specialization in Public Legal 
Sciences, a Master’s in European Union law, and an LL.B. Before joining the European 
Commission, Tiago worked as a lawyer in various international law firms. He is also 
frequently involved in research projects and lecturing commitments. 
This year, continuing a tradition, JURIX has also been accompanied by satellite 
co-located events: five workshops – CLAIRvoyantS, AI4Legs-V, NLL2FR2025, AI4EVIR, and AI4A2J – and the Doctoral Consortium.  
CLAIRvoyantS: 3° ConventicLE on Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Safety  
explored topics such as the impact of the AI Act on high-risk and sensitive sectors (e.g. the judicial, legal, and health domains), and questions whether AI tools are currently transparent, accurate, and trustworthy enough.  
AI4Legs-V: The 5th Workshop on AI for Legislation  discussed challenging 
questions involving the use of AI and technology in general to support the legislative process, with interdisciplinary instruments coming from the philosophy of law, 
constitutional law, legal informatics, including AI and law, computational linguistics, 
computer science, HCI, and legal design.   
NLL2FR2025: Translating Natural Legal Language into Formal Representation  
brought together researchers and practitioners interested in bridging the gap between natural legal language and formal representations, but the focus of the workshop extended beyond the translation of natural language rules into logical formulae to 
include the formalisation of legal cases described in natural language.  
AI4EVIR:  AI for Evidential Reasoning  aimed to bring together researchers working 
on formal, computational, and empirical approaches to reasoning with evidence, as 
well as those with expertise in forensic science and evidence evaluation. The goal of the workshop was to foster discussion and exchange between theoretical and applied 
perspectives on how AI can contribute to evidential reasoning in legal and investigative 
contexts.  
AI4A2J: AI for Access to Justice, Dispute Resolution, and Data Access  invited 
legal technologists, researchers, and practitioners to discuss how innovations in AI can help to close the access to justice gap: the majority of legal problems go unresolved vii

around the world because potential litigants lack the time, money, or ability to 
participate in the court processes which could solve their problems. The workshop had 
three main tracks: i) Data issues related to access to justice (building reusable, shareable datasets for research), ii) AI for access to justice generally, and iii) AI for 
dispute resolution. 
Organising this edition woul d not have been possible without the support of many 
people and institutions . Special thanks are due to Francesca Grasso (Local Chair), 
Rachele Mignone (Web and Social Media Chair), Ivan Spada and Federico Torrielli 
(Tech Chairs), and the local support team of the University of Turin, Davide Audrito, Marinella Quaranta, Ilaria Angela Amentea, Marianna Molinari, and Stefano Locci. 
We would like to thank the workshop organisers for their proposals and for the effort 
involved in organising the events. We owe our gratitude to Monica Palmirani, who kindly assumed the function of Doctoral Consortium Chair this year as well. We are 
particularly grateful to the 107 members of  the Programme Committee for their work in 
the rigorous review process and for their participation in the discussions.  
Finally, we would like to thank Jaromír Savelka and Michal Araszkiewicz for their 
advice, and the current JURIX General Board for their support and for taking care of 
all JURIX initiatives.

Abstract.   Research in AI and Law has traditionally focused on case-based reasoning in common law systems, 
where factual similarity and factor-based modeling dominate. Much less attention has been given to continental 
jurisdictions, where judicial decisions are formally non-binding but still exert significant interpretive influence. This paper investigates how precedents function as interpretive resources in statutory reasoning, using the 
Polish Supreme Court decision as a case study. We use the case frame method, which structures judicial 
reasoning into slots: interpreted provision, competing interpretations, supporting arguments, meta-rules, and final decision. By applying this model to the source case and its reception in later case law, we identify three 
recurring patterns: (i) cross-domain influence, where the interpretive meta-rule travels across criminal, 
administrative, and transitional justice contexts; (ii) different takeaways, where distinct interpretive holdings (e.g., evidentiary standards, procedural guarantees) are extracted from the same judgment; and 
(iii) modificatory application, where courts cite the precedent but reshape its operative force.
 
Keywords.  Case-based reasoning, Case frames, Continental legal systems, Precedent, 
Statutory interpretation 
1. Introduction 
AI and Law research has developed rich models of case-based reasoning (CBR) in the 
context of common law jurisdictions, where stare decisis makes earlier judicial decisions 
formally binding. Much of this work has focused on factor-based representations of cases 
and on methods for reasoning about similarities and differences between fact situations [1-8]. By contrast, continental legal systems, where statutes are primary sources of law 
and precedents are formally non-binding, have received much less attention in case-
based modeling until recently [9, 10]. Here, the use of earlier cases arises not primarily from factual analogy but from interpretive reasoning: courts cite and rely on prior 
decisions as persuasive authorities for construing statutory terms. Existing factor-based 
CBR models are ill-suited to capture this practice, since the decisive question is typically not whether current facts resemble those in earlier cases, but how statutory provisions 
were interpreted and eventually applied. 
To model such reasoning, this paper adopts the Case Frames approach [10], which 
represents cases in terms of their interpretive structure: the provision at stake, the interpretive methods employed, the competing readings considered, the meta-rules 
invoked, and the final decision. Case frames allow us to see how courts make use of earlier judgments in statutory interpretation.

The contribution of this paper is as follows. It demonstrates the effectiveness of 
the case frames method  in structurally presenting the content of cases under continental 
law and in tracing how subsequent courts make use of earlier decisions. Our manually 
crafted dataset, consisting of 33 judgments citing the landmark Polish Supreme Court 
decision V KK 74/08,2 reveals three recurring patterns: (i) cross-domain transfer of an 
interpretive meta-rule, (ii) reliance on different holdings embedded in the same decision, 
and (iii) modification of the transferred meta-rule. Together, these patterns highlight 
argumentation practices in continental legal culture that differ significantly from those 
in common law and contribute to the theoretical foundations of AI and Law by enabling the study of distinctive forms of precedent use in statutory systems. 
The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 introduces the case frame method and 
explains the simplified representation employed in our analysis. Section 3 presents the source case V KK 74/08  and reconstructs its interpretive content. Section 4 examines its 
reception in later judgments, distinguishing three characteristic modes of citation and adaptation. Section 5 discusses the implications for AI and Law, situating our findings within the literature on case-based and rule-based reasoning. Section 6 concludes and 
outlines directions for future work, including the integration of case frames with formal 
methods of legal knowledge representation including the Semantic Web technologies, and large language models. 
2. 
Case Frames Method 
In statutory legal systems, once the evidentiary facts are established, the crucial legal 
question usually turns on how to interpret the wording of the applicable statute. 
Precedents therefore function less as repositories of factual patterns and more as sources 
of interpretive knowledge. To capture this knowledge, we use the case frame method, a structured representation of judicial reasoning in interpretive disputes. 
For the purposes of this study, we employ a simplified version of the case frame 
model [10]. Each case frame records the following elements: 
 Case name: unique code identifying the case. 
 Interpreted provision: the statutory clause or term at issue. 
 Competing interpretations: alternative readings considered by the court. 
 Arguments: the interpretive methods invoked (e.g., linguistic, systemic, 
purposive). 
 Meta-rule: the second-order directive governing the relationship between 
methods (e.g., primacy of linguistic interpretation, holistic combination). 
 Final decision: the interpretation ultimately adopted. 
This representation allows us to observe how courts cite and reuse earlier cases. A 
later decision may transfer a case frame in its entirety, but often only selected 
elements are borrowed. For example, a court might cite a precedent to adopt its meta-rule while ignoring its specific interpretation of a provision, or conversely, invoke the 
same statutory interpretation but change the justificatory arguments. Case frames thus 
provide a fine-grained lens through which to study cross-domain transfers and modifications of precedents in continental legal jurisdictions.

In the sections that follow, we apply this model to analyze the reception of a 
landmark Polish Supreme Court’s judgment. By reconstructing case frames for the 
source case and for the later cases that cite it, we can show how interpretive knowledge travels across doctrinal boundaries, sometimes intact, sometimes transformed. 
3. 
Source Case: V KK 74/08 
 
The judgment V KK 74/08 of the Polish Supreme Court (18 November 2008) arose from 
a cassation in a homicide case. The defendant had been convicted of murder, and one of the key issues concerned the recidivist aggravator in art. 148 § 3 k.k. This provision 
imposes harsher penalties when the perpetrator commits homicide after having already 
been convicted of “murder” (PL: zabójstwo). The problem was whether a prior conviction for a privileged form of homicide — for example, killing under strong 
emotional disturbance — also counts as “murder” for the purpose of this aggravator. 
This was not a trivial question. If “zabójstwo” were read broadly to cover all forms 
of homicide in the Code, then even someone previously convicted in mitigated circumstances would face aggravated punishment if convicted again. But if the term were 
read narrowly, limiting it to the basic and qualified types of murder, then those with a privileged prior conviction would not fall under the aggravator. The interpretive dispute 
thus turned on whether the legislature intended “zabójstwo” to be a blanket reference to 
all types of homicide, or a more selective reference consistent with the internal structure 
of the Criminal Code. 
The Supreme Court’s resolution of this issue made V KK 74/08 a landmark decision. 
It began with a linguistic analysis, noting that the wording could be understood in more than one way. Because the linguistic outcome was not univocal, the Court turned to 
systemic reasoning: privileged homicide provisions exist precisely to mitigate liability, and treating them as aggravating factors would contradict their function. From this, the 
Court drew the broader principle that linguistic interpretation is the starting point but not 
the end point of statutory reasoning. Even where terms appear clear, their meaning must be tested against systemic and purposive considerations. Let us note that this is one 
among many possible meta-rules governing the sequence of application and the 
preference relations between different interpretation canons [11,12]. 
Beyond this interpretive canon, the judgment also addressed procedural guarantees 
(prohibition of reformatio in peius), the standard of proof in circumstantial cases, and 
the scope of clerical error correction. These holdings, although ancillary in the original case, would later be invoked independently by other courts. The following Table 
expresses the crucial interpretive problem of the case.

4. Reception of V KK 74/08 in Later Case Law 
The significance of V KK 74/08 lies not only in its original resolution of a homicide provision, but also in the way later courts have cited and adapted it. In Continental legal  
systems, precedents are formally non-binding, yet they often serve as interpretive 
resources. What is striking in this line of reception is not merely that later courts quote V KK 74/08, but that they do so in markedly different ways. In order to trace the 
reception of V KK 74/08, we created a dataset of 33 cases citing it. The citing cases were 
identified on the basis of hyperlink system available in the LEX database: one of the leading electronic commercial repositories of Polish legal resources. All citations of the 
source cases were identified and their structure analyzed by an experienced lawyer. Three 
patterns emerge: Cross-domain influence  – the case is cited outside criminal law, for example in 
administrative and transitional justice proceedings, illustrating that precedents in continental legal culture can be mobilized across doctrinal boundaries. Different takeaways from the same case  – later courts may extract distinct elements of 
the case frame (e.g., the interpretive meta-rule, the standard of proof, or the guarantee against reformatio in peius ), treating them as independent resources. 
Modificatory application  – courts sometimes narrow or transform the very element 
they cite, producing outcomes that differ in spirit from the original decision. M. Araszkiewicz / Precedent as Interpretive Resource 5

Each of these phenomena can be represented through case frames, which make visible 
which elements are transferred, which are omitted, and which are reshaped. In the 
following subsections, we illustrate each pattern with examples. 
4.1. Cross-Domain Influence 
The most striking feature of the reception of V KK 74/08 is the extent to which 
its interpretive meta-rule, according to which linguistic primacy does not imply exclusivity, and that even seemingly clear terms must be tested against systemic and 
purposive arguments, has been mobilized beyond the original context of homicide law. 
In criminal law, the decision has been cited not only in later homicide cases, but also 
in disputes concerning other provisions of the Criminal Code, such as the interpretation of “possession” in drug offences or of “significant quantity” in narcotics law. In each 
instance, courts explicitly referred to V KK 74/08 to justify the methodological move from literal wording to systemic and purposive arguments. This shows that the meta-rule 
has become a general meta-rule of statutory interpretation, detached from the original 
dispute over homicide provision.  
The meta-rule has also travelled into administrative adjudication, where courts and 
other authorities have faced questions of statutory inter pretation under regulatory 
statutes. In such settings, V KK 74/08 has been cited to stress that reliance on apparent linguistic clarity is insufficient: the statutory term must be construed in considering its 
systemic context and purpose. 
The precedent has influenced cases concerning the status of repressed persons under 
the 2015 Act on opposition activists. Here, the term “harm” ( szkoda ) in art. 3 pkt 3 lit. b 
raised an analogous interpretive issue: does it require actual realized detriment, or can 
politically motivated attempts at repression also qualify? By invoking V KK 74/08, the 
Supreme Administrative Court underscored that interpretation could not stop with the 
linguistic reading but had to integrate systemic and purposive considerations.

 In sum, the reception of V KK 74/08 across criminal, administrative, and transitional justice cases confirms both the portability and flexibility of its holistic canon. The same 
methodological directive—testing linguistic meaning against systemic and purposive 
considerations—travels easily across domains yet does not dictate uniform results. Depending on the balance of arguments, it may justify either a broadening  (as in I KZP 
9/11 on security measures) or a narrowing  (as in III OSK 732/21 on the notion of harm) 
of statutory terms. This dual character demonstrates that the meta-rule is used as a framework for disciplined reasoning, one that accommodates divergent but 
methodologically consistent outcomes. 
4.2. Different Takeaways from the Same Source Case 
While V KK 74/08 is most frequently cited for its holistic canon of interpretation, later 
courts have also drawn on its other holdings, each of which resolved an interpretive issue under different statutory provisions. These include the standard of proof for 
circumstantial evidence (art. 7 CCP), the prohibition of reformatio in peius  (art. 443 
CCP), and the scope of clerical error correction (art. 105 CCP). 
Under continental law assumptions, such holdings have no binding force: they are 
ancillary to the main ruling and are not meant to structure future case law. Nevertheless, 
practice shows that they are transferred virtually 1:1 into subsequent decisions. Courts cite these passages of V KK 74/08 as if they were stable interpretive authorities, 
confirming their persuasive weight in shaping juridical consensus. The below table

4.3. Modificatory application 
The mere fact that a court cites V KK 74/08 does not guarantee that the holistic 
interpretive canon is transferred in its original form. Citation can be a misleading signal: 
while the authority of the precedent is invoked, the substantive element being transferred may be reduced or redirected. A striking example comes from II AKa 447/12, where the 
appellate court formally acknowledged V KK 74/08 but confined the use of systemic and 
purposive interpretation to situations where linguistic interpretation itself does not resolve the interpretative issue—that is, only when the text itself allows at least two 
different readings. This move effectively narrowed the meta-rule, stripping it of its 
broader function in V KK 74/08, where systemic and purposive considerations were required even when the wording seemed clear. To present this phenomenon in a clear 
manner in the table below we contrast the narrowing reading of the meta-principle (as 
applied in II AKa 447/12) with faithful transfer of the meta-rule which took place in 
another case, V KK 119/10.

This comparison illustrates that citation of V KK 74/08 can serve different strategic 
purposes. In some instances, as in II AKa 447/12, the precedent is invoked mainly to 
anchor authority, while its operative force is curtailed. In others, like V KK 119/10, the canon is transferred intact and used to expand the statutory meaning. Importantly, 
modification need not always be restrictive: courts could also make the canon more open-
ended by broadening the range of permissible systemic or purposive arguments, or by introducing additional interpretive elements. What remains constant is the dual function 
of citation—both as a gesture of continuity with established authority and as a vehicle 
for recalibrating interpretive freedom. 
5. Discussion 
For AI and Law, our findings suggest the need to move beyond factor-based models of 
case-based reasoning that dominate analyses of common law precedents. Unlike the Anglo-American context, where the central task is identifying factual similarities and 
differences, in continental legal culture statutory law, the key unit of transfer is the 
interpretive element: a reading of a provision, a set of competing arguments and a meta-rule about how interpretation should proceed. Case frames provide a natural 
representational tool for this setting, as they decompose judgments into slots [13] that 
can be selectively reused in later cases. 
This insight resonates with earlier work by Rissland and Skalak, who emphasized the 
importance of modeling open-textured concepts and flexible interpretive strategies in case-based reasoning systems (CABARET) [14, 15]. Their approach underscored that 
legal reasoning frequently involves applying or modifying abstract interpretive heuristics 
rather than simply matching factual patterns. Our analysis confirms this observation within a statutory, continental legal culture: courts do not merely “follow facts,” but 
rather transfer, reframe, and sometimes narrow or broaden interpretive statements and 
meta-rules across doctrinal boundaries. 
The semi-formal representation developed here complements these insights. By 
explicitly representing interpretive slots—provisions, competing interpretations, arguments, meta-rules, holdings—case frames provide a richer structure for encoding how open-textured legal terms are resolved in practice. Recent research highlights that 
large language models (LLMs) can be leveraged to identify and reason about open-
textured terms in statutes [16]. Our approach complements this line of work: whereas LLMs can help detect where open-texture arises, case frames capture how 
courts resolve  such open-texture by mobilizing interpretive arguments and meta-rules. 
Such research should also relate to the earlier work concerning identification of elements 
of case law useful for statutory interpretation [17].

6. Conclusions and Further Research 
This paper has shown how the case frames method can capture the structural reuse of 
interpretive reasoning in continental legal systems, using the landmark decision V KK 
74/08  and 33 judgments citing it as a dataset. The analysis identified three recurring 
patterns of reception—cross-domain transfer of interpretive canons, reliance on additional holdings, and modificatory applications—which together demonstrate that precedents in statutory cultures function primarily as sources of interpretive 
resources  rather than binding commands. Case frames, by decomposing cases into 
provision, competing interpretations, arguments, meta-rules, and holdings, offer 
a transparent, systematic and replicable way to study these dynamics. 
A further contribution of this work lies in its methodological direction, which appears 
promising for practical applications. The case frame tables were generated with the assistance of ChatGPT-5, based on carefully designed prompts explaining the method, 
and then validated by an expert lawyer. This workflow illustrates how LLMs can assist 
in extracting structured representations from raw judicial texts, while human expertise ensures legal accuracy. The result is a semi-formal dataset that bridges the gap between 
textual judgments and formal models of legal reasoning, motivating the development of 
hybrid legal applications useful for legal practice [22]. 
Although primarily analytical rather than experimental , this research provides a 
foundation for systematic experimentation with  LLMs on case datasets. Future work 
could explore how models can be trained or fine-tuned to generate reliable case frames 
automatically, to detect interpretive issues, and to predict which elements of a source 
case are likely to be transferred, modified, or ignored in later decisions. This would complement ongoing work on open-textured statutory terms by enabling computational 
tools not only to identify interpretive uncertainty but also to model how courts resolve it. 
Further research should also pursue three broader directions. First, building a larger 
corpus of case frames  would allow for quantitative analysis of how interpretive 
arguments and meta-rules propagate across domains. Second, aligning case frames 
with formal knowledge representation  methods and reasoning models would make it 
possible to test the expressive power of existing solutions (e.g. [23]) against real-world 
interpretive practices. Third, by encoding case frames in machine-readable formats  (e.g. 
RDF), they could be integrated into  Semantic Web environments  and leveraged 
in retrieval-augmented generation systems [24], offering structured, high-quality resources for AI systems trained on legal texts. 
Taken together, these avenues point toward a hybrid research agenda: case frames 
provide a jurisprudentially meaningful unit of analysis  while also serving as 
a computationally useful resource , bridging doctrinal insight and AI-supported modeling 
of statutory interpretation in continental legal systems. M. Araszkiewicz / Precedent as Interpretive Resource 11

JuriDiscovery: Automated Analysis of
Legal Dispute Triggered by Public
Policies Using Artiﬁcial Intelligence
A Case Study Applied to the Individual Microentrepreneur
Loreane BRANDIZZIa,1Guilherme RODRIGUESa,2
aUniversity of Bras ´ılia, Brazil
Abstract. The litigation arising from weaknesses in the implementation of pub-
lic policies in Brazil has become a growing challenge. Among the many affected
groups, Individual Microentrepreneurs (MEI) represent a signiﬁcant case, withthousands of lawsuits addressing rights, obligations, and structural shortcomingsof this regime. Analyzing such cases is complex due to the large volume and un-structured nature of judicial data. Advances in Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI), particu-larly Large Language Models (LLMs) and semantic clustering, offer opportunitiesto transform legal texts into structured knowledge. This study presents a pipelinethat combines BERTopic and prompt engineering to extract and analyze judicialcases involving MEIs. The results highlight recurring issues such as employmentrelationships, social security beneﬁts, free legal aid, tax exemptions, and registra-tion fraud. The methodology proved robust, scalable, and adaptable to other judi-cial contexts, contributing to both academic research and decision-making in publicadministration and legal practice.
Keywords. Jurimetrics, Legal Analytics, Public Policies, Natural Language
Processing , Large Language Models, Topic Modeling
1. Introduction
Guided by its Digital Government Strategy, Brazil has advanced a transformative agenda
for public administration and the economy, ranking 14th worldwide in the United Na-tions 2023 index of digital public services [1]. Yet, evaluating Brazilian public policiesremains complex: traditional methods such as surveys, while robust, are costly, time-consuming, and unable to capture the dynamic nature of social impacts [2]. This gapmakes policy evaluation itself a structural challenge. The Individual Microentrepreneurregime, established by Complementary Law No. 128/2008 [3], is an example of a com-plex public policy. It allows self-employed workers and small business owners to for-malize their activities under a simpliﬁed tax and social security framework. Fifteen yearsafter its creation, the regime has generated a lasting legacy of judicial disputes, makingit a relevant case study for this research.

Rather than relying solely on traditional surveys and economic models, policy eval-
uation can beneﬁt from judicial data, where conﬂicts and system failures are formally
recorded. Legal disputes often provide an X-ray of unresolved problems, as illustrated bythe billion-dollar fraud in unlawful social security discounts at Brazil’s INSS, which hadbeen signaled for years through thousands of lawsuits and complaints before erupting inApril 2025 [4,5,6] . To detect hidden problems of this scale before they erupt, jurimet-rics, combined with advances in AI, offers transformative potential. The integration ofstatistical methods with NLP and LLMs has revolutionized legal data analysis [7,8], andthis work contributes by applying LLMs to unstructured judicial data and enhancing thesemantic representation of case summaries.
This work proposes to analyze the impact of the MEI policy within the judiciary and
to show how modern AI techniques can automatically uncover the main issues arisingfrom its implementation. Our main contribution is the development of a pipeline that ap-plies Topic Extraction, enhanced with LLM-based prompt techniques, to transform thou-sands of unstructured judicial decisions into semantically organized and interpretable in-formation. The method improves topic modeling by generating clearer and less redun-dant labels, enabling the identiﬁcation of litigation patterns linked to public policy im-plementation. In addition to the analytical pipeline, we also provide a visualization toolthat makes the results accessible to stakeholders interested in evaluating public policies.
The proposed approach is parameterizable, enabling its adaptation to different con-
texts of policy judicialization while supporting evidence-based decision-making.
2. Related Work
Jurimetrics combines statistical methods and data science to Law [9]. In Brazil, studies
highlight its use in legal research [10] and in decision support [11]. More recently, theﬁeld has advanced with the application of AI and LLMs [7,8,12,13].
The rise of LLMs has accelerated the use of AI in jurimetrics, enabled by the Trans-
former architecture [14], advances in computational infrastructure, and the availabilityof large-scale datasets. In the legal domain, speciﬁc models such as LawGPT, ChatLaw,LexiLaw, and JurisLMs have been developed for tasks like summarization and deci-sion classiﬁcation [7,8]. In Portuguese, initiatives such as LegalBERT-pt [12] and Juris-BERT [13] show the adaptation of these models to local contexts. Recent works, includ-ing CaseEncoder [15], SAILER [16], and LawGPT [17], highlight the growing sophisti-cation and diversiﬁcation of legal-domain language model architectures.
Despite progress, unstructured legal data remain difﬁcult to process due to their
lack of standardization and inherent complexity [7]. This challenge, recognized by theBrazilian Judiciary in the recent Manual for Standardization of Case Summaries [18],underscores the need for specialized modeling and data curation.
LLMs are increasingly used in legal data pipelines for tasks such as summariza-
tion and information extraction, supported by prompt-engineering strategies like PromptChaining [19], Chain-of-Thought [20], and In-Context Learning [21], enabling zero-shotsummarization without explicit training [22,23].
The use of LLMs in jurimetrics is well established; however, their exclusive adop-
tion raises concerns about interpretability, bias and reproducibility [24]. To mitigate theseissues, unsupervised topic modeling remains a alternative for large-scale legal text anal-L. Brandizzi and G. Rodrigues / JuriDiscovery 15

ysis. Among such methods, BERTopic [25] stands out for generating semantically coher-
ent and interpretable clusters, with comparative studies conﬁrming its superiority overclassical models such as LDA, NMF, and Top2Vec [26]. BERTopic can be enhancedthrough the integration of LLMs, which reﬁne topic labeling via prompt-based methodsthat produce clearer labels [25]. This same synergy has been explored in recent workssuch as TopicGPT [27] and TNT-LLM [28].
Recent studies conﬁrm BERTopic’s effectiveness in legal text analysis across juris-
dictions. Didwania et al. [29] compared it with LDA and NMF on Indian and UK judicialdocuments, ﬁnding similar coherence scores but higher semantic quality in expert evalu-ations. Likewise, Aouichaty et al. [30] analyzed nearly 200,000 Arabic legal judgments,showing that domain-speciﬁc monolingual embeddings achieved higher topic coherenceand, overall, conﬁrming BERTopic’s suitability for large-scale legal corpora even whenusing standard Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and Hierar-chical Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (HDBSCAN) set-tings.
Building upon these insights, the present study adopts BERTopic for its maturity and
interpretability, combining it with domain-adapted prompts for label reﬁnement, summa-rization, and structured insight generation in Portuguese judicial texts, using BERTim-
bauas the embedding model [31].
3. Methodology
The proposed methodology is parameterized, allowing easy adaptation to other datasets.
It consists of ﬁve stages (Figure 1) and is based on 57,075 Brazilian judicial casesummaries explicitly mentioning “Microempreendedor Individual”. The data were web-scraped from public sources and stored in a database, containing only case summariesand metadata (case number and court), with no personally identiﬁable information.
Figure 1. Executed stages of the pipeline.
Approximately 96% of the case summaries contained between 100 and 20,000 to-
kens, ensuring sufﬁcient textual depth for analysis. Four large-context LLMs ( codestral-
22b, pixtral-12b, deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-14b, and llama-3.1-8B-instruct )
were tested via the SERPRO [32] LLM API on a stratiﬁed sample of 200 cases us-ing a common summarization prompt. Evaluations considered format and content cri-
teria, with the latter veriﬁed through an LLM-as-a-judge approach using GPT-3.5.
Pixtral-12B [33] achieved the best balance and was selected for subsequent stages.
3.1. Information Extraction
Exploratory analysis showed that many mentions of MEIs in the case summaries were
contextual, appearing in legal citations or references to related provisions, rather thanL. Brandizzi and G. Rodrigues / JuriDiscovery 16

indicating that the MEI was directly involved as a party. This required an initial ﬁltering
step to identify cases where the MEI effectively participated in the dispute.
To ensure consistency and extract relevant information from the summaries, the texts
were standardized following the Manual for Standardization of Case Summaries [18].A prompt, which included a one-shot example to guide formatting, was applied to bothreformat the summaries and verify MEI involvement (Figure 2), conﬁrming participationin11,775 of the 57,075 analyzed cases.

3.2. Metadata Enrichment
Metadata were obtained through the public DataJud API [34], with endpoints identiﬁed
according to each case’s court of origin. For MEI-related cases, metadata were success-fully retrieved for 9,786 records, including details such as case type, jurisdiction level,
municipality code, judging body, legal subjects, ﬁling date, and procedural history.
3.3. Topic ExtractionThe concatenated texts from the ﬁelds descricao

were vectorized using BERTimbau for all cases in which MEI involvement was con-
ﬁrmed. The resulting embeddings were then clustered semantically with the BERTopic
library [25].L. Brandizzi and G. Rodrigues / JuriDiscovery 17

The BERTopic model was conﬁgured with its default hyperparameters, which com-
bine dimensionality reduction through UMAP with the HDBSCAN algorithm. While
HDBSCAN was used with its default settings, the UMAP parameters were customized
(nneighbors=30, ncomponents=5, mindist=0.15, metric=‘euclidean’) to re-
duce noise and improve topic separation.
Following clustering, BERTopic identiﬁes topics using a frequency-based TF-IDF
representation restricted to each cluster. It can also leverage LLMs for topic labelingthrough prompts applied to centroid documents and keywords. In this study, that strategywas adopted with speciﬁc adaptations described in the next step.
3.4. Cluster Labeling:Cluster labeling was performed through prompt engineering, instructing the LLM to in-
fer labels from a representative set of documents. The prompt integrated three compo-nents: (i) TF–IDF topic keywords, (ii) the texts of the documents closest to each clustercentroid, and (iii) concise instructions in Portuguese. We employed the Pixtral-12B
model via an external API (outside the standard BERTopic pipeline), sending one request
per cluster with the prompt illustrated in Fig. 3 (translated from Portuguese).
For each cluster, labeling was based on the documents nearest to its centroid (in
terms of cosine distance). To ensure the representativeness of this subset, kmembers
were selected, deﬁned as k=min{max(⌈ρ n⌉,15),100, n}, where ρ=0.30 and nis the
cluster size.
Figure 3. Prompt for Topic Labeling (translated from Portuguese).
In an alternative to the standard BERTopic workﬂow, which uses another prompt and
a limited set of integrated LLMs, we invoked Pixtral-12B externally, applying a cus-
tom prompt and contextualized examples for topic labeling. Representative documentswere selected proportionally to cluster size and based on centroid proximity.
3.5. Cluster GroupingOnce the topic clusters were obtained, a veriﬁcation stage evaluated potential dimen-
sionality reduction, as some topics presented semantically similar names. Embeddingsof each topic label were generated using BERTimbau, and cosine similarities were com-
puted to form an N×Nmatrix, where Ncorresponds to the total number of topics. Topic
pairs with similarity above 0.75 were then submitted to the Pixtral-12B model with aL. Brandizzi and G. Rodrigues / JuriDiscovery 18

legal prompt (Figure 4) to conﬁrm whether they represented the same issue. The model
produced binary responses (“1” or “0”), resulting in a ﬁnal binary N×Nmatrix of the-
matic equivalence.
Figure 4. Prompt for Identifying Whether Two Topics Represent the Same Legal Issue
After constructing the similarity and binary matrices, a graph-based grouping strat-
egy was applied to merge topics representing the same legal issue. Each topic was treated
as a node, and groups were incrementally formed through a greedy and strict process: atopic was included only if it was connected in the LLM validation matrix (1) and showedcosine similarity above 0.75 with all existing members. This procedure substantially re-
duced topic redundancy while preserving semantic precision. In each group, all relatedcases were updated in the database with the metadata of the most representative topic,deﬁned as the one with the largest number of associated cases.

3.8. Ablation Study and Evaluation
To assess the effectiveness of each methodological stage, an ablation study was con-
ducted. The data were clustered with BERTopic while systematically varying three fac-
tors: dataset (full corpus vs. MEI-ﬁltered cases), textual input (original ementa vs. sum-
marized description and issues) and methodological techniques (without LLM labeling,
with LLM labeling, and with LLM-based grouping).
Topic coherence across stages was measured using the Normalized Pointwise Mu-
tual Information (NPMI) [35], which quantiﬁes word co-occurrence within a ﬁxed con-text window for a topic’s top terms. Values range from [−1, 1], with higher scores indi-
cating stronger semantic associations and, therefore, more coherent topics.

5. Conclusion
5.1. DiscussionThe developed pipeline proved effective in generating automated and meaningful in-
sights into the judicialization of public policies. By combining topic extraction tech-
niques with LLMs, it transformed unstructured legal texts into interpretable analytical in-
formation. The approach performed well in the MEI policy context and, being parameter-ized, can be adapted to other judicial domains, supporting the identiﬁcation and analysisof temporal, spatial and semantic patterns of litigation.
No manual validation or human labeling was used, ensuring reproducibility and
adaptability to other contexts. Rather than revalidating BERTopic’s well-established per-
formance, this study extends it to the legal domain, combining its clustering capabilities
with LLM-based label reﬁnement and semantic grouping.
The proposed pipeline progressively enhanced data quality and interpretability, with
each stage [from prompt-based extraction to clustering, labeling, and grouping] incre-mentally reﬁning the representation of judicial cases. A key methodological contribution
lies in extending BERTopic through customized topic labeling and contextual grouping,
which substantially improved clustering coherence and interpretability, as evidenced by
the ablation study.
The integrated use of LLMs signiﬁcantly enriched the labeling of topics and the
generation of high-quality descriptive summaries, making the data more accessible, un-
derstandable and actionable for analysts, public managers and researchers.
5.2. Limitations and Future WorkOne limitation of this study concerns HDBSCAN’s sensitivity, which classiﬁed 31% of
cases as noise, reducing the analysis sample. Although prompt-based reclassiﬁcation was
tested, it compromised visualization clarity. Nevertheless, excluding borderline cases im-
proved semantic homogeneity and coherence within clusters.
To mitigate LLM related risks (bias, misclassiﬁcation, and over-simpliﬁcation) four
models were tested and evaluated by an independent LLM using the same prompt, en-
suring the selection of the most accurate and contextually faithful model.
Another constraint stems from the dependence on the quality of case summaries.
Very short entries were excluded to preserve analytical integrity. Despite being non-
exhaustive, the dataset’s size and diversity support reliable generalization of trends in
MEI-related judicialization.
Future research may extend this pipeline to other public policy domains, such as
social security, healthcare, and education.L. Brandizzi and G. Rodrigues / JuriDiscovery 23

Abstract. One of the most important legal assessments during legislative drafting
proposals in Parliament is to check whether the bills have some provisions clashing
with the Constitutional norms. Sometimes this situation is intentionally created bythe proposer of a party to underline inconsistencies or incompleteness in the legalsystems according to the reality of the society, but frequently, they are mistakes toavoid. This paper presents a method to calculate a multi-factor index of presump-tion of unconstitutionality of the provisions of a bill, to inform the proponent con-cerning a possible constitutional conﬂict. The paper uses a large dataset of bills,coming from the Chamber of Deputies of Italy, combined with Constitutional Courtjudgments and abstracts, EU and National legislation (9095 Italian laws, 3710 bills,2979 judgments from the Constitutional Court). The methodology used is hybrid,considering different technological components, linked in a pipeline: i) embeddingsimilarity; ii) normative references navigation; iii) semantic topic of the bill; iv)legislation cited in the judgments score based on the abrogated.
Keywords. Constitutional law, embedding, Akoma Ntoso, similarity, sentence
transformer
1. Introduction and Research Questions
Constitutional review is a cornerstone activity of modern democratic governance aimed
at ensuring that legislation aligns with the foundational principles enshrined in a nation’sconstitution. While ex post constitutionality review is usually demanded to specialised
high-level courts, it is also carried out ex ante (i.e., before the bill is approved) by Par-
liaments on bills under discussion, to prevent the unconstitutionality of the forthcom-ing text. Such preliminary constitutionality review is traditionally carried out through le-gal scrutiny by parliamentary committees and designated departments of civil servants.However, the increasing complexity of legislative proposals and the evolving sociopoliti-cal landscape suggest the possibility of integrating Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) systems insupport of the parliamentary activities for this speciﬁc task. law foundations [1] - e.g., separation of powers, the autonomy of the decision-maker[2], the law-making process - shall be conjugated with technical solutions that ensureaccountability, fairness, and explainability of the outputs [3].
In this study, we investigate the feasibility of a novel automated assessment method
of the constitutionality of bills while conjugating legal principles and the peculiarities oflegal texts. We focus on the Italian legal system, a civil law country in which a Constitu-tional Court is tasked with an ex post assessment, and in particular on the activities of the
Chamber of Deputies, one of the two branches of the Parliament, that has the obligationto check the possible unconstitutional provisions.
Given these premises, this study aims to investigate the following research questions:
• RQ1. How is it possible to represent the text of a bill with embedding while re-
specting its structure (paragraphs, subparagraphs, etc.) and navigating normativereferences point in time? This is a preliminary objective that will allow us to com-pare the bill with other material (e.g., decisions of the Constitutional Court).
• RQ2. How is it possible to fruitfully retrieve relevant decisions from the Italian
Constitutional Court, given the text of a bill? This objective allows us to identifythe decisions to compare with our bill.
• RQ3. How is it possible to compare a bill and the relevant decisions, and then to
measure the risk of a bill being unconstitutional, given the bill and the correlatedrelevant decisions of the Constitutional Court?
To tackle these challenges, this study relies on a hybrid approach which combines
an XML-structured representation of the legislative text in Akoma Ntoso and subsym-bolic approaches leveraging on this structure [4]. Owing to the novelty and experimen-tal nature of the approach, our results should be interpreted as preliminary, yet they arenonetheless encouraging. The paper is divided as follows: following this introduction,Section 2 introduces the background and the motivation underlying the study; Section 3describes the datasets, whereas Section 4 details the methodology. Experimental settingsare presented in Section 5, while their results are presented in Section 6 and discussed inSection 7. Some conclusive remarks are reported in Section 8.

However, this task is not very well studied by the scientiﬁc research, that has con-

Predicting courts decision is a classic task of the ”AI & Law” domain [5,6]. Rele-

Surveys show a consistent pattern of duality: on the one hand, certain studies focus
on case law retrieval from higher courts and have the goal of retrieving pertinent to aset of facts (in most cases) or a given piece of legislation [13]; on the other hand, somestudies focus on the constitutionality assessment as a classiﬁcation task in which thestudy’s goal is to predict the outcome of the Court’s decision given a set of facts orprior cases [14]. This can happen with or without the case retrieval. Large LanguageModels (LLM) are showing advances in both ﬁelds [15,16,17], despite the chance ofhallucinations[18] and technical constraints (e.g., context length).
Our study differs from the existing literature on three grounds:
•it focuses on the Italian legislative system, which has not been subject to particularattention in the domain of unconstitutionality evaluation. This might be due toseveral reasons, including data retrieval and language complexity;
•it processes bills rather than in-force legislation or sets of facts. While trainingdatasets of the existing literature use applicable legislation, we directly measurethe risk of unconstitutionality over bills. The difference lies on the fact that in-force laws are already interpreted by lower courts and constitutional courts haveprior interpretations at their disposal. From a legal standpoint, assessing the con-stitutionality of bills is harder when compared to applicable legislation;
•it uses an XML-enriched version of the legal texts to allow the point-in-time nav-igation of legal references, rather than plain text. This contributes to increase theproximity between the reasoning performed by the automated system and the oneperformed by the Constitutional Court.

4. Methodology
Our approach is to build a meaningful index of unconstitutionality for CD Italian bills
according to legal principles and considering the similarity of the bill with the relevantdecisions of the Constitutional Court that have already decided unconstitutionality. Whilean alternative approach could have lead to ﬁnd similarities between the current bill andlegislation already scrutinised by the Court, this would have lead to the inclusion oflegislation already assessed and, in turn, some degree of bias towards the prediction.Therefore, we have considered three parameters: the similar domain, the similar legalconcepts, and the similar rationale in the legal reasoning.
In order to produce a meaningful measure of the risk of unconstitutionality, the ﬁrst
step is to match bills with the relevant judgments from the Constitutional Court. Onemight be tempted to use a lexical comparison based on TF-IDF or similar techniques.These approaches, however, rely on the assumption that the lexical overlap between thetwo documents being compared is signiﬁcant. In the case of the comparison betweenbills and constitutional court judgments, these are very different types of documents,which have a different structure an lexicon. For this reason, our approach is based ona sentence transformer [19], a type of model which allows the creation of embeddingsfor sequences of text, which can then be used to ﬁnd semantically similar texts. Thisis typically achieved by using a contrastive learning loss, which forces the vectors forsimilar sentences to have a high cosine similarity.
While sentence embeddings can be used to compare the semantics of relatively short
portions of text, the ability of any model to deal with longer documents is not guaranteed.In fact, even LLMs struggle with documents, recent results show that the effective lengthof most documents is lower than the maximum number of tokens by at least an order ofmagnitude [20] and they are effectively able to deal with less than 10k tokens. To producea meaningful semantic similarity metric between Italian bills and Italian ConstitutionalCourt judgments, we considered the following portions of these documents:
• CD Italian bills: by leveraging the Akoma Ntoso format we are able to access theM. Corazza et al. / Unconstitutionality Prevention in Bills Using Hybrid AI 29

5. Experimental Settings
From the technical point of view, our goal is to compare the three similarity metrics dis-
cussed in Section 4 and to assess the overall feasibility of this approach. We opted to useone of the multilingual models from SentenceBERT, namely “paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2” [21]. This model is trained from a monolingual Sentence Transformermodel, namely “paraphrase-mpnet-base-v2” which is based on MPNet [22]. The adoptedapproach is based on the teacher-student paradigm, where the goal is to produce a modelwhere the original and translated versions of the same sentence have a high cosine simi-larity.
In order to assess the performance of our approach, we tasked an expert in consti-
tutional law to produce a list of 10 bills that involve different topics. Then, the expertperformed a preliminary analysis by annotating relevant decisions that could be used toassess the risk of unconstitutionality for each bill. In particular, the focus was the cre-ation of a list of subjects that potentially involve matters of constitutionality, and a listof judgments that are the most important precedents for each subject. Then, the expertmanually checked the 10 most similar judgments to each selected bill, as produced bythe three similarity metrics. Finally, the 10 most similar judgments were annotated aseither “relevant” or ”not relevant”.

6. Results Evaluation
To measure the performance of the various similarity criteria, we used recall as a metric,
since we have access to the ground truth judgments provided by our expert, as wellas those that are within the top 10 and top 5most similar judgments to a given bill.This choice of 10 and 5 judgments was motivated by a mediation between providingusers with as many relevant results as possible, while not overwhelming them with toomany, which would make the method less useful. The results of our evaluation are shownin Table 4 and they show the recall of the system when using the top 10 and top 5most similar judgments, respectively. Since we do not have access of a complete listof true positives, as this would require an extensive and time-consuming exploration ofall the constitutional court judgments, we are unable to calculate the precision of thesystem. In our experiments, the comparison between bill articles and the paragraphsof the motivation proved unsuccessful. This can perhaps be explained by the fact thatthis comparison involves many different portions of text, which makes it less reliable.Furthermore, the differences in language between a judgment and a bill might also haveimpacted the performance. The comparison between Chamber of Deputies Commissionsand ratio decidendi from the Court also proved unsuccessful. This result might be due
to the fact that the scope of each Commission is very broad, meaning that some detailsabout the speciﬁc bills cannot be represented correctly. Finally, our best results comefrom the comparison between bill articles and abstracts from the Constitutional Court,which is probably due to the more concise and simpler language used in the abstractwhen they are compared with the overall judgments. Furthermore, since each verdict isassociated with its own abstract, this further enhances the granularity of the approach,allowing the embeddings to be more accurate.
7. Discussion
In order to deepen our understanding of the shortcomings of our approach, we conducted
a post hoc legal analysis of the results. Firstly, we observed that in two cases (Term Limitsfor Elected Ofﬁces and Criminal Penalties for Drug Offences), our system was unableto retrieve any relevant judgments. From a legal perspective, both bills made only veryM. Corazza et al. / Unconstitutionality Prevention in Bills Using Hybrid AI 34

speciﬁc modiﬁcations to highly technical existing legislation. Speciﬁcally, the bill on
term limits for elected ofﬁces consisted of a single substantive article and contained onlyone explicit reference to the area of legislation affected by the modiﬁcation. This suggeststhat our methodology performs better when the theme of the legislation is repeatedlyexpressed within the legislative texts, whereas it tends to struggle when the context mustbe inferred primarily through normative references. Secondly, in the case of the bill onchildren’s surnames, the system was able to retrieve all the relevant case-law annotatedby our expert. This bill, while modiﬁcative in nature, amends the Civil Code, which is aparticularly structured type of legislation, with a set of topics that are generally mutuallyrelated and with semantically informative article titles. Thirdly, when comparing truepositives and false negatives, it can be observed that the approach struggles to identifythe most recent relevant judgments. In many cases (e.g., end-of-life or employment rightson termination), the system identiﬁed some relevant case-law but missed the most recentjudgments on the matter. This limit is legally signiﬁcant because of the evolving natureof constitutional case-law, which requires constitutionality analyses to begin with thejudgments that best reﬂect the approach of the sitting court. Finally, the system suggestedjudgments that were not annotated ex ante by our expert but were considered relevantin the post hoc analysis. This highlights that very complex, time-consuming, and open-ended legal tasks, such as researching the relevant case-law to assess the constitutionalityof bills, can beneﬁt from assistive AI-based applications, which are capable of processinglarge volumes of information in a short amount of time.
8. Conclusive Remarks
This paper demonstrates an innovative hybrid pipeline to calculate an index of unconsti-
tutionality of the bills of the Chamber of Deputies of Italy. We have fostered the AKN-XML annotation of the heterogeneous legal sources repository, using embeddings to pre-pare vectors for similarity comparison. We have also combined different levels of simi-larity to grasp different aspects of the legal principles in the Constitutional Law to sup-port the unconstitutionality analysis. The results are promising, but we intend to addmore levels of legal analysis in the future. We aim to improve our work, including Ques-tion/Answering knowledge graphs coming from the legal knowledge of domain. Sec-ondly, we intend to annotate some ratio decidendi with an ontology in order to improve
the embeddings with RAG based on supervised legal knowledge. Thirdly, we will startan in-place evaluation made by legal experts of the Chamber of Deputies to capture morereasoning models to inject in our system. Another improvement could be a time-sensitivemodeling of the unconstitutionality index, which would consider crucial temporal as-pects such as the weight of abrogated norms. Finally, we intend to further improve andvalidate our results by including articles of the Constitution in the analysis.

Abstract. Legal decision-making requires comprehensive legislative knowledge
and up-to-date case information. Legal Knowledge Graphs can enhance accessi-
bility of such information, support semantic querying, and serve as knowledge-intensive components for predictive machine learning applications. To address thelimited availability of legal KGs, this work develops a KG focused on cases ofviolence against women. Two complementary construction approaches are pre-sented: a bottom-up, domain-customized methodology and a novel Large Lan-guage Model-based solution. Both integrate data extraction, ontology development,and semantic enrichment using sentences from the European Court of Justice assources. The resulting KGs are validated through competency questions and showpotential to improve access to legal information, enable complex queries, and pro-vide a valuable knowledge backbone for supporting predictive tasks such as caseoutcome analysis.
Keywords. Knowledge Graph Generation, Large Language Models, Linked Data,
Semantic Web, Violence Against Women, Prediction.
1. Introduction
In recent years, the legal domain has witnessed an increasing usage of solutions based
on Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) to effectively manage the legal consultation and decisionprocess [1,2]. Despite the advancement of legal technologies [3], there is a signiﬁcantgap in the availability of structured and easily queryable resources tailored to the legaldomain, such as Knowledge Graphs (KGs) [4]. Current KGs in the legal domain oftendo not address speciﬁc subtle challenges, particularly with regard to interoperability,semantic richness, and adaptability to predictive tasks [5,6].
A legal KG must be able to cope with the speciﬁc and intricate writing style of laws
and sentences and keep track of their evolution, including exceptions and applicability.Legal Knowledge and Information Systems

We address the urgent global phenomenon of violence against women2,a violation of hu-

tively countering this problem requires coordinated actions from governments, civil soci-ety, and individuals. Our work contributes by developing advanced tools and knowledgeresources, particularly knowledge graphs, to support the analysis of judicial reasoning,facilitate policy evaluation, and improve access to structured case-law data, on gender-based violence. To this end, we introduce a novel Legal KG, speciﬁcally designed toaddress judicial cases related to violence against women, along with the methodologiesadopted for its development.
The Legal KG is automatically derived from the jurisprudence of sentences of
the European Court of Human Rights
3(ECHR), targeting cases of gender-based vio-
lence. It adheres to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data prin-
ciples. The resource is built upon two methodologies: a customization of the generalKG development process to the legal domain [8] (with a bottom-up solution combin-ing data extraction, ontology development, and semantic enrichment through alignmentto domain-speciﬁc ontologies), and a new approach to automated KG generation, basedon the exploitation of Large Language Models (LLMs), as recent advancements have
opened up new possibilities for automating and improving various phases of ontologydevelopment[9], that could be customized to the legal domain. The two methodologiesproduced complementary results: the former provided more precise outcomes, but ismore computationally expensive while the latter is more scalable, but ensured less ac-curacy. The obtained resource has also been validated via suitable CQs (CompetencyQuestions) [10].
Besides being the ﬁrst result addressing the ECHR case law to cases of violence
against women, the Legal KG may serve as a proxy for broader applications. Judicialpronouncements prediction can be thus viewed a link prediction problem within the Le-gal KG. This approach can be generalized to other domains, provided that legal KGs aregenerated through the proposed methodologies.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Sect. 2 reviews the state of
the art on legal informatics, KGs and ontologies in law. Sect. 3 presents a customizationto the legal domain of the bottom-up KG development process and the resulting LegalKG. Sect. 4 presents a new approach for automated KG generation, grounded on theexploitation of LLMs and customized to the legal domain, and the obtained Legal KG.Sect. 5 discusses the results and the effectiveness of the adopted methodologies. Sect. 6concludes the paper by outlining future research directions.

4. Legal Knowledge Graph Construction: LLM and NLP Pipelines
Recent LLM advances have transformed Natural Language Processing (NLP) by en-
abling ontology development, knowledge graph construction, and query answering.
These models enhance accuracy and efﬁciency in information extraction, addressing lim-itations of traditional knowledge engineering methods [21]. These models can augmenttraditional approaches by leveraging extensive training data to infer relationships, iden-tify patterns, and construct meaningful representations of unstructured textual data, suchas court rulings and legal documents.
Legal document analysis technology based on LLMs, with the semantic understand-
ing capacity and contextual modeling ability, may effectively tackle these challenges andprovide powerful auxiliary tools for [22]. This synthesis of LLM and KG enables betterunderstanding and generation of structured information, addressing long-standing chal-lenges in the ﬁeld. Developing legal KGs is challenging due to the domain complexity.This approach combines LLMs for ontology generation and data extraction with tradi-tional NLP for structured, precise text processing. Integrating both methods into a uni-ﬁed pipeline enables the creation of accurate, comprehensive KGs aligned with domainrequirements and validated using CQs.
Effective prompt engineering [23] is essential for leveraging LLMs to produce de-
sired outputs. This approach utilized two key techniques: zero-shot prompting, suitable
for simple tasks with clearly expressed requirements, and few-shot prompting, which in-
cludes examples to guide the model in handling more complex tasks and reducing errorslike hallucination.
4.1. KG DevelopmentThe proposed methodology for generating KGs from legal rulings integrates advanced
LLMs and traditional NLP techniques into a cohesive workﬂow. It involves twopipelines, one of which is an NLP-based pipeline
25.The LLM pipeline includes docu-
ment preparation, RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) development, ontology andKG creation, and competency question validation, while the NLP pipeline focuses onpreprocessing, POS tagging, and triple extraction for constructing KGs.

4.1.1. LLM’s Pipeline
Document Preparation: The case study focused on analyzing and constructing KG from
legal judgments, considering two distinct types of input. The ﬁrst type utilized the en-
tire judgment (full-text), while the second involved a speciﬁc sub-part of the judgment,selected by domain experts. The aim was to assess the effectiveness of both input types.For preparation, automated functions were used to extract text from PDFs for the full-text input. However, due to the varying structure and complexity of each judgment, man-ual extraction was employed for the sub-part input. Once the text was extracted, it wasformatted into a document, ready for the subsequent steps.RAG’s Creation: RAG models have been employed to limit the output of LLMs to
the context of each speciﬁc document. Although LLMs are trained on vast amounts ofdata, sometimes they struggle with providing accurate responses to specialized tasks.To address this issue, RAGs enhance traditional LLMs by integrating well-deﬁned cor-pora [24], enabling LLMs to access two types of data when responding to user queries:parametric data, which refers to the model’s training data, and nonparametric data, whichconsists of new, external data stored in a vector container. The LLM inspects this non-parametric data to generate precise answers. For the creation of RAGs, the TogetherEm-bedding method
26from the LangChain library was used. BERT-M2 served as the embed-
ding model for semantic search within the vector dataset, and FAISS27,accessed through
the langchain_community library, was used to manage the vector dataset. RAGs werecreated for all ﬁve documents involved, which were then used as the contextual basis forthe LLM to generate responses to various prompts.Base’s Ontology Creations: At this stage, the ontology, serving as a T-box for con-
structing the ﬁnal KGs, was developed. Initially, GPT-4.o was employed to generate afoundational ontology, as Mixtral 8x22b proved incapable of creating a general schemafor this topic. Using GPT-4.o resulted in a basic ontology containing core elements suchas classes (e.g., Abuse and LegalCase) and ObjectProperty. Subsequently, the ontology
was enriched with additional elements using Mixtral, which, despite explicit instructionsin the prompts, tended to add extra components like DataProperty and ObjectProperty
during the KG generation process. To further reﬁne the ontology, a zero-shot promptingtechnique was applied to domain-speciﬁc documents. Prompts instructed the model toexpand the ontology by incorporating fundamental concepts from these documents. Thisprocess was repeated with several randomly selected documents and, after multiple iter-ations, it was observed that Mixtral consistently produced similar elements regardless ofthe input document. This indicated structural similarities among the documents, allowingthe newly generated elements to be reused across them, effectively identifying commonpatterns. Once the ontology was ﬁnalized, a thorough review was conducted to eliminatesuperﬂuous elements in the schema. This step addressed inconsistencies and redundan-cies in DataProperty elements, ensuring the alignment with the project requirements.
KG Creation: Building on the created ontology and the RAG for each document, a
prompt engineering phase was undertaken to generate KGs for each document. Thisphase utilized a few-shot prompting technique to design effective prompts. Once the in-dividual KGs were generated, they were merged into a uniﬁed graph. The merging pro-

4.1.2. NLP’s Pipeline
Preprocessing: This step, as described above, was conducted to evaluate and compare
new LLM-based approaches. The process was applied to only one of the ﬁve previously
analyzed documents. Initially, after the document was read and its text extracted, a pre-processing phase was carried out using the NLTK library
28.This phase involved several
steps, including punctuation removal, tokenization, stopword removal, and lemmatiza-tion, to prepare the text for subsequent analysis.Part of Speech: After tokenization, the SpaCy library was used to perform POS tagging
for each token. POS tagging is a NLP technique that categorizes the components ofa sentence, making it particularly valuable for complex tasks like Sentiment Analysisor Machine Translation. In this study, POS tagging was utilized to extract triples fromthe document. Tokens were categorized into "subj" (subject), "verb," and "obj" (object)based on their grammatical roles, enabling the creation of structured triples.Triples Creation: Finally, triples were constructed by associating each identiﬁed subject
with its corresponding verb and object. This process resulted in a structured representa-tion of the text, capturing meaningful relations between entities within the document.
4.2. Empirical Evaluation and ResultsThe LLM-based KG generation was qualitatively evaluated using CQs. Across 5 doc-
uments with 13 CQs each, full text inputs produced 61.5% consistent answers, while
28https://www.nltk.org/C. D’Amato et al. / Automated Creation of a Legal Knowledge Graph Addressing Cases 44

sub-part inputs yielded 56.9%. This shows a trade-off: full-text offers broader coverage,
whereas sub-parts provide more focused and relevant results, particularly for factual orprocedural queries, offering insight into the KG structure, coverage, and correctness.
This approach assesses LLMs in knowledge engineering tasks such as ontology gen-
eration, instance creation, and comparison with traditional NLP methods. LLMs strug-gled to create complete domain-speciﬁc ontologies using only pretrained knowledge, re-quiring additional documents and expert oversight. While the generated ontologies gen-erally performed well, instances were sometimes incomplete or inaccurate, highlightingthe need for human validation. Two speciﬁc use cases were explored to evaluate the ef-fectiveness of LLMs in document processing:1)Full-text approach: This use case involved processing the entire document to construct
KGs and answer CQs. While this approach provided the highest quantity of responsesdue to its comprehensive coverage, the relevance and accuracy of the responses varied.Full-text processing captured more nuanced information but required signiﬁcant manualveriﬁcation to ﬁlter out irrelevant or incorrect outputs. The technical challenges includedlonger processing times and token size limitations inherent in LLMs.2)Sub-part approach: The approach used expert-selected text segments to focus on the
most relevant content. While it generated fewer responses than using the full text, it wasfaster, avoided token limits, and better aligned with expert objectives, though it relied oncareful expert input to avoid missing important information.
The evaluation of the CQs (Tab. 2) emphasized responses aligned with the text,
excluding incomplete entities generated solely by the LLM. The resulting KG, availablein the GitHub repository
