2. Guidelines, Annotation Process, and Corpus
The source data consists of 101 preliminary rulings of the CJEU in the V A T domain, on
the subtopics of taxable amounts and exemptions for the public interest. Of these docu-ments, resulting from a concept-based search using the EUR-Lex Directory
3in Decem-
ber 2024, 21 were manually labelled, while 80 were labelled automatically.
The annotation guidelines were drafted and iteratively improved following in-depth
theoretical and empirical analysis of formulas as used in the argumentative style of theCJEU. As a general rule, we deﬁne a JIF as an interpretative statement by the Court,either formulated for the ﬁrst time or drawn from cited case law. Since the objective isto extract the interpretative statements attributable to the Court, annotation focuses onthe part of the decision containing the Court’s answer to the preliminary question, whichlies between the ﬁrst occurrence of “Consideration of the question referred” (or similarexpressions) and the section on litigant costs (introduced by “Costs”). The annotationunit is one paragraph, reﬂecting the typical structure of CJEU judgments, which areorganised in numbered paragraphs, each expressing an autonomous step of reasoning[11]. In most cases, JIFs have purely legal content, i.e. interpretation of law or legalprinciples in abstract terms, without any reference to case-speciﬁc facts. However, JIFsmay occasionally contain factual issues, such as in the ﬁnal part of the decision, where

2.1. Manual Annotation Method
We created our guidelines and corpus through multiple stages of annotation, each involv-
ing different documents and methodologies, as reported in Table 1. The guidelines wereenvisioned not only as instructions for human annotators, but also as a potential sourceof information for automated annotation methods. To maximise their effectiveness, theguidelines included examples taken from existing documents. Since this provides a clearadvantage for automatic annotation on those same texts, it required careful partitioningof the corpus to ensure sound downstream evaluation. In particular, the test split containsonly documents that were never used during the development of the guidelines.
The ﬁrst draft of the guidelines was based on theoretical and empirical studies. Two
annotators jointly worked on a shared set of documents (set A), iteratively reﬁning theguidelines until no ambiguities remained. To validate the guidelines, the annotators thenindependently annotated a new set of decisions (set B), in a double-blind process. Dis-agreements were discussed and resolved, leading to a consolidated version of the guide-lines. A third set of decisions (set C) was then independently annotated by both annota-tors and used to validate this ﬁnal version. We measured the Inter-Annotator’s Agreement(IAA) on set C at paragraph level, restricted to the relevant portions of the judgments.The resulting Cohen’s κ[12] was 0.96, indicating almost perfect agreement.
Since the guidelines were reﬁned after annotating sets A and B, and thus relied on
examples from documents contained therein, these sets were excluded from the test splitand merged to form the validation split. Conversely, the guidelines remained unchangedafter annotating set C, which was included in the test split, further increased by includinga fourth set of decisions (set D), with each document annotated by a single expert.

Results indicate that Transformer models generalize well, achieving performance
comparable to or even better than DeepSeek. They also exhibit behaviors similar to thoseobserved for the three generative LLMs on the validation set, namely higher recall andlower precision on the positive class, with DeBERTa showing the most pronounced dif-ference. This can be explained considering that the models were trained over data anno-tated using DeepSeek. Therefore, it is reasonable to speculate that they may have learnedsimilar patterns and a tendency to favour false positives over false negatives. Moreover,the models show stability across repeated runs, as indicated by the low standard deviationof the results. LinearSVC’s performance is not much inferior to state-of-the-art models,suggesting that lexical cues play a crucial role in the task.
In general, we consider LEGAL-BERT to be the best model. It is the most stable,
and it has the best macro F1 score as well as the best F1 score in the positive class.Moreover, it has the second-best recall score over the positive class, close to the best.This is particularly relevant for tools intended for legal practitioners, as the presence ofadditional JIFs is preferable to the absence of fundamental ones. Indeed, users can easilydiscard a few irrelevant paragraphs, but cannot know if a crucial JIF is missing.
4. Conclusion
In this paper, we presented a machine-learning framework for the extraction of JIFs from
CJEU decisions on V A T cases. We leverage the capabilities of LLMs for annotatingtraining data and explore the performance of various classiﬁers in this domain.
A general limitation of using LLMs in the legal domain lies in their proprietary na-
ture and lack of transparency, as well as susceptibility to hallucinations [15]. However,our approach mitigates these issues by using a dedicated, task-speciﬁc classiﬁer for theﬁnal extraction of JIFs, combining the strengths of LLM prompting with a more trans-parent and reproducible model. Our results indicate that the annotations produced auto-matically by LLMs can be exploited to distil LLM knowledge in much smaller modelsthat obtain comparable results, reducing annotation costs and improving scalability. Byenabling large-scale extraction of these statements, our approach helps various stake-holders, including judges, practitioners, and scholars, in reviewing EU case law.G. lenging when abbreviations map to multiple candidate laws, yet it is crucial be-

We presenta self-supervised, graph-based method that constructs a weighted co-occurrencegraph from court decisions, where nodes are legal provisions and edge weights re-ﬂect their co-occurrence frequency. Ambiguous references are resolved by mea-suring distances from context provisions using a multi-source Dijkstra algorithm,selecting the closest candidate.
Experiments show that the approach improves accuracy over naive baselines,
provides conﬁdence scores for reliability, and delivers a practical disambiguationmethod, while our study also contributes an annotated dataset for future research.
Keywords. legal provision extraction, graph-based disambiguation, co-occurrence
graph, court decisions
1. Introduction
Parsing references to statutes and legal provisions in legal texts is essential for turning
unstructured documents into structured, machine-readable data. In legal texts, referencesoften appear as
§〈paragraph〉〈 section〉〈 letter〉〈 act name〉〈 local alias〉
§ 34 section 5 letter a) Criminal Code (hereinafter, ‘CC’).
Once an alias is declared, later mentions of the abbreviation (e.g., CC) are unam-
biguous within the document; without an alias, the shorthand may refer to multiple acts—the ambiguity we aim to resolve.
Regular-expression and rule-based methods reliably detect such references and list
candidate acts but often fail to disambiguate the abbreviation.
Here, the correct act must be inferred from the surrounding context (e.g., neigh-
boring provisions, recurring terminology, co-occurring references). Existing approachestypically rely on supervised learning with annotated data [1] or on semantic similaritybetween text embeddings [2].
An alternative is to prompt large language models, but these are resource-intensive.
We therefore explore a lightweight method that exploits the structural regularities of le-gal texts, using LLMs only for low-conﬁdence cases. This hybrid design reduces costsLegal Knowledge and Information Systems

Our contributions are threefold:
•We propose a self-supervised graph-based method, built on co-occurrence patterns
of legal provision references, to resolve ambiguous references in court decisionsand output prediction conﬁdence scores.
•We evaluate the method on a curated dataset of Slovak court decisions, showingimproved accuracy over naive baselines.
•We release the annotated language-agnostic dataset to support further research inlegal text processing.
2. Related Work
Legal reference extraction has traditionally relied on regular expressions and other rule-
based methods; Palmirani et al. (2003) showed that such approaches, which match sur-face patterns, perform well on well-structured references [3]. Van Opijnen et al. (2015)introduced xLLx, a rule-based system for extracting legal references from Dutch courtdecisions, which emphasized better maintainability than regular expressions and in-cluded handling of “local aliases” of law names [4].
More recent approach introduces machine learning: Darji et al. (2023) frame legal
reference prediction as a classiﬁcation task, using BERT-based models to predict the cor-
rect law reference from candidate mentions in German court decisions [5].
Graph-based models have also gained traction in legal AI. Zhang et al. (2023) pro-
posed the Missing Link model, a GNN for joint citation prediction combining semanticand topological features [6], and Fujita et al. (2022) explored hypergraphs for hierarchi-cal and self-referential citation modeling [7].
Unsupervised and self-supervised methods are particularly relevant in low-annotation
domains. LamBERTa,a BERT model trained on the Italian Civil Code, leverages unsu-
pervised labeling for extreme classiﬁcation (i.e., tasks with thousands of possible labels)[8].
While prior graph-based legal work (e.g., Boulet’s code networks [9], Hier-
SPCNet [10]) emphasizes document similarity or hierarchy. Our approach adopts a self-supervised paradigm but differs from prior graph-based methods by focusing on co-occurrence graphs of legal provisions, modeling their contextual relationships for disam-biguation.
3. Dataset Overview
Our experiments are conducted on a dataset of court decisions, speciﬁcally designed to
support the development and evaluation of legal reference disambiguation. The dataset isdivided into two distinct parts: a graph-building set (containing only parsed law refer-
ences without disambiguation) for constructing the co-occurrence graph, and an evalua-
tion set (ambiguity-labeled) for testing the disambiguation method. We ﬁrst describe the
evaluation set, so the reader clearly understands the disambiguation task, before detailinghow the graph-building set is constructed.Š. Horvát et al. / A Self-Supervised Method for Legal Reference Resolution 301

Evaluation Set The evaluation set mimics the real-world disambiguation task. Instances
were generated by our rule-based extractor [11]: when a local alias was absent and only a
law code abbreviation was present, the system consulted a dictionary of possible codes. Ifmultiple candidates existed, the extractor could not resolve the reference. Each instancethus contains the same structural detail (paragraph/section/letter) but multiple candidatecodes from this dictionary. Candidates that did not contain the referenced detail in theactual legislation were discarded, ensuring that all remaining alternatives are valid pro-visions.
The correct provision for each instance was annotated by a domain expert, who
inspected the surrounding decision text and selected the provision matching the legalcontext. This process yielded 123 disambiguation instances.
Each instance represents an ambiguous shorthand reference (e.g., “CC”) that could
refer to multiple acts containing an identically numbered provision (e.g., both the Crim-inal and Civil Codes might have a §34). Each includes the correct answer and severalplausible, yet incorrect, options. The structure is shown in Table 1.

4. Methods
We tackle the legal reference disambiguation problem using a self-supervised, graph-
based method that exploits co-occurrence patterns of legal provisions. The approach hastwo main stages: graph construction and reference disambiguation.
Graph Construction The core of our method is a weighted undirected graph G=(V,E)
built from the training set:
• Nodes ( V): Each distinct legal provision occurring in the corpus is represented as
a node.
• Edges (E ): An edge is added between two provisions if they appear together in
the same court decision.
• Edge Weights: The weight of an edge is the number of co-occurrences of the con-
nected provisions across the corpus. Higher weight therefore indicates a stronger
association.
This graph can be constructed efﬁciently without manual annotation: for each court
decision in the graph-building set, we take the set of co-occurring legal provisions fromthelaws attribute and increment the edge weight for every pair.
To improve robustness, we apply edge ﬁltering controlled by a threshold τ
edge: all
edges with a co-occurrence count below τedgeare removed1,as they likely reﬂect noise
or rare coincidences.
Disambiguation Given the co-occurrence graph, we disambiguate legal references in
the evaluation set as follows:
1.Context Nodes Selection : From each ambiguous instance, we collect surround-
ing provisions in the ﬁelds laws before andlaws after. These context provi-
sions serve as source nodes for distance computation.
2.Distance Computation: Using a multi-source variant of Dijkstra’s algorithm
[12], we compute the shortest-path distance2from all context nodes to every other
node in the graph.
3.Score and Select: For each candidate provision cincandidates, we compute
the sum of its shortest-path distances from all context nodes:
score(c)= ∑
ctx∈contextdistance(ctx, c).
The candidate with the smallest score (i.e., closest to the context) is selected asthe predicted resolution.
The scores can be inverted and normalized to yield conﬁdence estimates, which
quantify the relative closeness of each candidate to the context.

Matrix Co-occurrence Baseline As a simpler alternative to our graph-based approach,
we implement a matrix-based baseline that relies solely on direct co-occurrence counts.
We build a symmetric co-occurrence matrix M, where each entry Mijrecords how often
provisions iand jco-occurred in the same decision. During disambiguation, each can-
didate is assigned a score equal to the sum of its co-occurrence counts with all contextprovisions, and the candidate with the highest score is selected.
5. Experiments and Results
As some instances involve more than two candidates, a random baseline yields 47% ac-
curacy. A classic matrix-based co-occurrence baseline, which scores each candidate byits summed co-occurrence counts, achieves 69% accuracy. Our single predictor based ona co-occurrence graph achieves 76.4%, demonstrating that leveraging indirect connec-tions in the graph improves accuracy. An ensemble of 51 predictors—each built from500 random decisions—further improves performance to 79.7%.
Error Analysis Most errors occur when competing provisions frequently co-appear in
nearly identical contexts, limiting the signal available from co-occurrence alone. A typi-
cal case is the ambiguity between the 513/1991 Commercial Code (lex specialis) and the
40/1964 Civil Code (lex generalis), since commercial law prevails in business matters
but defaults to the Civil Code where it is silent.
Conﬁdence Analysis As expected, higher conﬁdence correlates strongly with correct-
ness. Predictions with conﬁdence <0.7 achieve 81% accuracy, those with conﬁdence
between 0.7 and 0.8 reach 91% accuracy, and predictions with conﬁdence ≥0.8 achieve
97% accuracy. This suggests that conﬁdence can be used to identify highly reliable pre-
dictions and ﬂag ambiguous cases for further review.
Implementation and the dataset are available at GitHub repository [13]. All experi-
ments were conducted in Python using Jupyter Notebook, with graph algorithms imple-mented via the networkx library [14].
6. Conclusion and Future Work
We presented a self-supervised, graph-based approach for resolving ambiguous le-
gal references in court decisions. By exploiting structural co-occurrence patterns, ourmethod outperforms naive baselines while requiring no manual annotation. Alongsidethe method, we contribute a curated dataset to support further research.
Future work includes integrating semantic information (e.g., surrounding keywords)
with the co-occurrence graph, exploring hybrid scoring strategies, and extending themethod to anomaly detection tasks, such as identifying misclassiﬁed legal references.

Abstract. To aid litigants’ appeal strategies, this study introduces Disputability
(δ), a novel metric quantifying a case’s contentiousness by the total number of judi-
cial instances it undergoes. Using a dataset of 52,993 Taiwanese tax judgments, we
test the hypothesis that similar cases share similar disputability levels. We compareJudgment-Level and Sentence-Level prediction models, ﬁnding that a Judgment-Level approach with multilingual-e5-base embeddings provides the strongest
and most practical baseline. While the Sentence-Level model suffered from signiﬁ-cant label noise, a high-precision kNN voting strategy proved particularly effectivefor identifying high-risk, disputable cases. Our work establishes an adaptable andextensible baseline for quantifying case disputability, offering a practical tool forcomputational law and legal analytics.
Keywords. Case Disputability, Legal Judgment Prediction, Baseline Model,
Computational Law, Machine Learning
1. Introduction
Whenever a lower court renders a judgment, the losing party invariably faces the decision
of whether to appeal. This deliberation is not limited to the loser; the prevailing party,as the potential appellee, must also consider the engagement of legal counsel, whichinvolves an inherent trade-off between litigation costs and potential beneﬁts. Researchby [1] suggests that, inﬂuenced by psychological effects, litigants are more inclined toretain legal representation only when the probabilities of winning and losing are nearlyequal. In other words, the contentious nature, or disputability, of a case impacts a party’sconsideration of litigation costs, thereby affecting their subsequent litigation behavior.
As for what inﬂuences a case’s disputability, consider a case that, having been ruled
upon by an intermediate appellate court (the second instance), is appealed to the highestcourt (the third instance), which then reverses and remands the second-instance judgmentfor further proceedings. This action necessarily implies a divergence in legal opinionsbetween the second and third instance courts; otherwise, the highest court would haveafﬁrmed the lower court’s decision. Thus, it is evident that a case’s disputability has astrong correlation with the number of judicial instances it undergoes. It can even be ar-gued that the disputability of a case is a causal factor inﬂuencing the number of instancesit passes through.Legal Knowledge and Information Systems

Based on these observations, we propose a quantiﬁable measure of case disputabil-

Deﬁnition 1.1 (Disputability). Given a case di, its disputability, denoted as δi, is deﬁned
as the total number of judicial instances the case has undergone before the ﬁnal and
binding judgment is rendered.
δi=Total number of judicial instances for case di
For example, if a case undergoes the ﬁrst instance, second instance, third instance
(reverse/remand), second instance (remand proceedings), and is ﬁnalized after a subse-quent appeal to the third instance (dismissal), it has passed through ﬁve judicial instances,and we deﬁne its disputability δ

Considering the practicalities of litigation, the plaintiff and defendant often cite
cases with similar facts but differing judicial outcomes as part of their arguments. Whilethe Civil Law tradition may allow for pure dogmatic analysis in the absence of prece-dent, it is more common to encounter similar cases with somewhat divergent viewpoints.Therefore, the second hypothesis of this study is that similar cases are likely to havesimilar disputability; in other words, cases similar to a highly disputable case are highlylikely to also be highly disputable.
However, the deﬁnition of “similar cases” has been subject to various discussions.
Past research has deﬁned case similarity from multiple perspectives, including legalfactors[2][3][4], dialectical reasoning[5][6], and hybrid methods[7], yet no single stan-dard has been universally adopted. This study attempts to utilize three different embed-ding models without any legal document ﬁne-tuning to deﬁne similarity based on Eu-clidean distance. This approach is intended to serve as a baseline model against whichthe performance of more specialized legal similarity measures can be evaluated, pre-serving the exploration of various similarity metrics for this problem. We then exam-ine whether this baseline modeling approach captures similar behavior in terms of dis-putability, speciﬁcally whether highly disputable cases are clustered closer together inthe Euclidean space.
2. Predictive Model Construction
When analyzing court judgments, regardless of a case’s disputability, certain common
phrases and boilerplate language are universally present. If judgments are directly em-bedded, it may be difﬁcult to ascertain which sentences signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the case’sdisputability. Consequently, we construct two distinct modeling approaches: one basedonJudgment-Level Embedding for disputability prediction, and the other based on
Sentence-Level Embedding, followed by aggregation for the ﬁnal prediction.

4. Concluding Remarks
Our study successfully introduced Disputability (δ
i) as a quantiﬁable metric based on
the number of judicial instances a case undergoes. The Judgment-Level models uti-
lizing multilingual-e5-base achieved the highest baseline performance, while the
Sentence-Based models, despite providing ﬁner granularity, suffered from signiﬁcantperformance degradation due to label noise.
The proposed model is highly extensible: its disputability deﬁnition, based on the
number of judicial instances, is easily adaptable across different legal domains and sys-tems. The framework can also ﬂexibly incorporate various case similarity metrics to en-hance interpretability and performance.
Our baseline model presents several notable limitations. Firstly, the current deﬁni-
tion of similarity based on Euclidean distance offers very low legal interpretability andis thus rarely suitable for direct practical use in legal contexts. Secondly, the Sentence-Based model proved overly susceptible to label noise. Effectively leveraging the bene-ﬁts of this ﬁne-grained processing requires either advanced data sampling techniques orsigniﬁcantly higher computational cost, which currently restricts its practical utility.
Future work should focus on two main areas. Firstly, for the Sentence-Based model,
research should be conducted to identify better sampling methodologies that allow themodel to perform robustly within smaller sample spaces, while simultaneously explor-ing various interpretable semantic similarity measures. Abstract. Court decision summarization is challenging due to the signiﬁcant length
and structural complexity of legal documents, which makes existing reinforcement
learning (RL)-based abstractive summarization methods less effective. We pro-pose an RL-based abstractive legal summarization model with a novel argument-structured reward mechanism. It leverages Issue–Reason–Conclusion componentsto compute ﬁne-grained sub-rewards and aggregate them into a ﬁnal reward. Thisdesign provides more reliable learning signals for model optimization. Experimentson the Indian Supreme Court dataset with Longformer-Encoder-Decoder (LED)and Llama demonstrate consistent improvements over non-argument-structuredmethods. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst work to incorporate argu-mentative structures into RL-based summarization, offering a novel direction forimproving legal summarization.
Keywords. Court Decision Summarization, Reinforcement Learning, Argument-
Structured Reward
1. Introduction
Court decision summaries are typically longer and more complex, which challenge cur-
rent summarization models, particularly for abstractive approaches that aim to generateconcise and coherent summaries. Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL)-basedmethods have shown promising performance in abstractive summarization. The currentreinforcement learning (RL) approach follows a two-stage approach: ﬁrst, supervisedﬁne-tuning (SFT) is used to obtain a baseline model; then RL training is applied to op-timize the model by maximizing pre-deﬁned reward. The reward can directly use eval-uation metric scores (e.g., ROUGE, BERTScore) or employ more sophisticated designs[1–3]. However, applying current RL methods to legal summarization reveals signiﬁcantlimitations. Previous work [4, 5] shows that current metric scores are brittle and high-variance for long or structurally complex summaries, thus providing unreliable signalsfor RL training in this setting. This raises a critical question: How can we design reward

that effectively capture the quality of legal summaries despite their length and structural
complexity?
To alleviate the aforementioned problem, we propose an RL-based abstractive le-
gal summarization model with argument-structured reward. Speciﬁcally, our method en-hances the reward signal with the argumentative structure Issue–Reason–Conclusion(IRC) in legal documents [6]. Our reward design involves three steps: (i) decomposeboth reference and generated summaries into argument-speciﬁc components; (ii) pair theargument-speciﬁc components from the reference and generated summaries and computea sub-reward for each argument-speciﬁc component; and (iii) aggregate the sub-rewardsaccording to their importance to obtain the ﬁnal reward. Intuitively, different argumen-tative components contribute unequally to the quality of a legal summary, and their im-portance should be reﬂected in the reward design. Notably, prior summarization work[7–10] has leveraged argumentative structures in supervised and unsupervised learning,whereas we focus on RL. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst work to incorpo-rate intrinsic argumentative structures into RL-based summarization methods.
We evaluate our argument-structured reward approach with LED and Llama models
on the Indian Supreme Court dataset. We compare model performance with and with-out the argument-structured reward, using BERTScore and ROUGE-L as training re-wards. Results demonstrate that our approach achieves consistent improvements overnon-argument-structured methods with both models and across both reward settings.With argument-structured reward, Llama achieves gains of up to 4.36, 5.09, 1.62 inROUGE-1/2/L scores and 0.48 in BERTScore, while LED shows improvements of 3.43,2.35, 1.83 in ROUGE-1/2/L scores and 0.73 in BERTScore.
2. Method
Our proposed method is shown in Figure 1, consisting of three principal steps: (1)
policy initialization, (2) argument-structured reward, and (3) policy optimization withargument-structured reward.Y. Kong et al. / Reinforcement Learning with Argument-Structured Reward 313

2.1. Policy Initialization
The policy is initialized by SFT on judgment–summary pairs. Under teacher forcing,
SFT minimizes the token-level negative log-likelihood. We then utilize the resulting SFTmodel to initialize the policy for the RL stage.
2.2. Argument-Structured Reward
To obtain more accurate reward for policy optimization, we propose a ﬁne-grained re-
ward mechanism that decomposes summaries into argument-speciﬁc components. Wecompute sub-reward for each component separately and aggregate them into a ﬁnal re-ward. Speciﬁcally, for each judgment, a summary is generated by the current policy.An argument role classiﬁer assigns one role in {I,R,C,O}(Issue, Reason, Conclusion,
Other) to each sentence in both reference and generated summaries. For each role in{I,R,C,O}, we form argument-speciﬁc components by concatenating the sentences la-
beled with this role in the original order. Then we compute the sub-reward for each com-ponent pair. For each summary, we thus obtain four sub-rewards. We assign a weight toeach sub-reward proportion to the size of the generated section. Intuitively, a role withmore tokens is considered more important and receives a larger weight in the total re-ward. The total reward is the length-weighted sum of sub-rewards.
2.3. Policy Optimization with Argument-Structured RewardGiven the total reward, we optimize the policy with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
[11]. To prevent the policy from collapsing and keep it close to the SFT reference policy,we consider the Kullback–Leibler (KL) penalty. We form the ﬁnal reward by combiningKL penalty term with the total reward. Finally, we employ PPO to update the policy.
3. Argument Role Classiﬁer
Legal summaries usually lack explicit argumentative annotations. To address this is-
sue, we ﬁrst leverage large language models (LLMs) to automatically generate pseudo-argument-role annotations, and then train an argument role classiﬁer on the LLM-generated data. The trained classiﬁer is subsequently used to assign argument roles tosentences in the summaries.
3.1. Multi-LLM AnnotationWe employ three LLMs to annotate argument roles at the sentence level. To ensure an-
notation reliability, we adopt a scheme with following three steps: (i) each summary issplit into sentences. The full summary is presented to the annotators so that each decisioncan be made in the context of the entire document; (ii) Gemini and GPT-4 independentlyannotate each sentence with one of four roles: Issue, Reason, Conclusion, or Other. Theyalso provide a brief rationale and a conﬁdence score. When two LLMs assign the samerole to a sentence, this role is directly adopted as the ﬁnal annotation for that sentence;(iii) when Gemini and GPT-4 disagree on a sentence, their rationales and conﬁdenceY. 6. Conclusion and Future Work
We proposed an argument-structured reward framework that leverages the intrinsic IRC

Abstract. Governance of marine genetic resources is fragmented across overlap-
ping treaties, creating uncertainty about which obligations apply in speciﬁc situ-
ations. 2. Related Work
The use of Hohfelds analytical framework in legal informatics has long been motivated
by the difﬁculty of expressing normative concepts without collapsing them into vaguecategories. Markovich [4] shows how Hohfelds schema can be formalised to preservethe relational and directed character of legal positions, arguing that precise differenti-R. Nanda et al. / A Hohfeldian Knowledge Base for LLM-Assisted Legal Information Retrieval 319

ation of deontic types is essential if computational models are to capture the logic of
legal relations without distortion. Francesconi [5], in turn, develops a semantic modelthat annotates and reasons over normative provisions, introducing patterns for Hohfel-dian relations and enabling both explicit and implicit norms to be retrieved across leg-islative texts. Peters and Wyner [6] develop a semi-automatic workﬂow that uses NLPtools and expert feedback to extract Hohfeldian relations from legal texts. Our work alsoconnects to legal question answering, a key use case of artiﬁcial intelligence and law(for early work, see, e.g., [7,8,9]). More recently, LLMs have been utilised to supportlegal question-answering. Approaches include using such models to support legal ex-pert systems (e.g., [10,11] asking a model to answer legal questions directly (see, e.g.,[12,13,14]), or connecting LLMs to more traditional information retrieval systems, e.g.,in a retrieval-augmented generation setup (see e.g., [15,16,17]).
3. Dataset
Dataset 1: Hohfeld-Structured Normative Knowledge Base (HSNKB): Two inter-
national law experts constructed the HSNKB from three core international instruments
governing biodiversity (CBD, NP, BBNJ-A). These treaties were selected because theyestablish the principal normative frameworks for access and beneﬁt-sharing (ABS) ofgenetic resources. Each row in the HSNKB represents a single operative clause (arti-cle, paragraph, or sub-paragraph) expressing one dominant normative relation betweenactors. Provisions containing multiple prescriptions were divided into separate entries,while preambular text, aspirational language, and deﬁnitional provisions were excluded.Each entry includes a unique identiﬁer, treaty name, provision number, the actor-holder,the legal position (or action), the actor-affected, and an expert-written natural-languagesentence describing the tripartite relation between actor-holder, legal position and actor-affected. Correlative positions are deduced based on Hohfeldian logic. HSNKB contains377 rows (193 from BBNJ-A, 96 from CBD, and 88 from NP), with “Contracting Par-ties” as the most frequent actor and “duty” as the dominant Hohfeldian relation.
Dataset 2: Fact Pattern Questions & Relevant Rows: We developed 15 fact-
pattern questions that connect the HSNKB to doctrinal reasoning for the legal informa-tion retrieval task. The relevant rows from the HSNKB that answer each question havebeen annotated as ground truth by an international law expert in marine biodiversity. Eachquestion is formulated according to the IRAC method: a scenario that presents actors and
circumstances, followed by an implicit issue, inviting identiﬁcation of the applicable ruleand analysis of its consequences. This format moves from straightforward single-treatyscenarios to more complex cases that require cross-referencing across multiple instru-ments. The dataset size is purposefully small to enable careful expert annotation. Weplan to expand its coverage and inter-annotator validation in future work.
Actor Deﬁnitions We compiled a dictionary of actor deﬁnitions linking names to
descriptions. This standardises references to implicit actors in fact-patterns and ensuresconsistent mapping across instruments.R. Nanda et al. / A Hohfeldian Knowledge Base for LLM-Assisted Legal Information Retrieval 320

4. Experimental design
To evaluate how well LLMs retrieve relevant treaty provisions from the HSNKB to an-
swer fact-pattern questions, we implemented two retrieval pipelines: full-scope retrievaland actor-constrained retrieval. In the full-scope retrieval, the model receives all HSNKBrows with three columns (unique identiﬁer, provision number and the natural languagesentence conveying the tripartite relation), along with supporting deﬁnitions (actor def-initions, explanation of Hohfeldian positions) embedded in the prompt and is asked toidentify the treaty provisions relevant to each fact pattern. In actor-constrained retrieval,the model ﬁrst identiﬁes the relevant actors in a fact-pattern, ﬁlters the HSNKB to candi-date rows involving those actors, and then retrieves the relevant rows from this reducedset. Both pipelines follow a zero-shot Chain-of-Instructions (CoI) [3] strategy. The sys-tem prompt instructions guide the model through four main stages: (i) parsing key enti-ties in the question such as actors, jurisdiction, resource type; (ii) applying jurisdictionalgating to avoid mixing provisions across regimes; (iii) applying an allocative ﬁlter to re-tain only provisions conferring Hohfeldian positions to the relevant actors; and (iv) ex-tracting HSNKB rows ranked by their speciﬁcity to jurisdiction, resource type, lifecyclestage, and traditional knowledge. For each question, the LLM is then asked to return theunique identiﬁers of the relevant rows in structured JSON format.
The pipeline is run with four different LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet
4, and Kimi K2) accessed via the OpenRouter
2API. All models were run in a zero-shot
setting, with temperature set to 0 (except GPT-5 which does not support the temperatureparameter), a ﬁxed seed, and response format as JSON. For the three reasoning models(Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4), the effort parameter was set to high so that themodel allocates a large portion of tokens for internal reasoning. The only expected outputis a dictionary of ranked unique identiﬁers corresponding to HSNKB rows. For eachof the 15 fact-pattern questions, the predicted unique identiﬁers (for rows) by the LLMare compared against the gold-standard rows. We utilise standard information retrievalmetrics: precision, recall, and F1-score. Macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-scoresare computed across all 15 questions, ensuring each question contributes equally to theoverall results. The dataset, code, and prompt are available at our GitHub repository

5. Results and Discussion
This section presents the results of our evaluation with respect to the research questions.
RQ1 examines how accurately LLMs retrieve the relevant rows from the HSNKB. In the
full-scope retrieval (see Table 1), GPT-5 attains the best performance, indicating strongselectivity with moderate recall. The three reasoning LLMs: GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, andClaude Sonnet 4 outperform the only non-reasoning LLM, Kimi K2. Across the twobest reasoning models, precision was modest, while recall was middling. Therefore, themain challenge is improving recall without reducing precision. Error analysis indicatesthat false negatives mainly involved conditional or multi-actor duties dispersed acrosstreaties, particularly those linked to beneﬁt-sharing obligations. False positives were lessfrequent and stemmed from the inclusion of programmatic cooperation clauses which gobeyond what was required by the fact-pattern.

6. Conclusion
This paper presented HSNKB, a fact-pattern dataset, and an evaluation of four LLMs us-
ing two retrieval pipelines. We compared two retrieval pipelines: full-scope retrieval andactor-constrained retrieval. The reasoning LLMs achieved modest precision and mid-dling recall. Actor-constrained retrieval yields limited gains over full-scope retrieval.Improving recall while keeping precision stable is therefore an important next step forcross-treaty retrieval. The error analysis of retrieval performance suggests that false neg-atives cluster around conditional and multi-actor duties, while occasional false positivesarise when cooperation language was interpreted as Hohfeldian duties. Future work willextend the dataset with more fact-patterns and include information retrieval baselines tobetter contextualize LLM-assisted retrieval.

Abstract. Retrieving relevant case law remains a time-consuming task. We com-
pare two embedding models for Czech Constitutional Court decisions: (i) a large
general-purpose OpenAI embedder and (ii) a domain-speciﬁc BERT trained fromscratch on ∼34,000 decisions. We introduce a noise-aware evaluation using IDF-
weighted keyword overlap as graded relevance, dual thresholds (0.20, 0.28),paired-bootstrap signiﬁcance, and nDCG diagnostics. Despite conservative abso-lute nDCG due to noisy institutional labels, the OpenAI embedder consistentlyand signiﬁcantly outperforms the domain BERT across all ranks and thresholds.Our framework enables robust evaluation under imperfect gold standards typical oflegacy judicial databases.

labels, Czech Constitutional Court
1. Introduction and Background
Searching for similar decisions constitutes a large part of the work of analysts, clerks, and
judges at the Czech Constitutional Court (ConC). We evaluate the feasibility of deployingautomated methods to support the retrieval of semantically similar decisions.
ConC provides public access to its case law via the NALUS database.
2Users typi-
cally retrieve cases by legal provisions or keywords. Currently, 713 keywords are manu-ally assigned to decisions by ConC staff, making the set a gold standard. However, staffturnover, the absence of formal rules, and emerging legal issues introduce noise and in-consistency over time. This problem is well known in Czechia, but its impact, includingfor automation, remains understudied.
We compare a domain-trained BERT with a general OpenAI embedder across three
embedding-based retrieval methods and propose an evaluation tolerant to noisy gold:IDF-weighted keyword overlap, two data-driven relevance thresholds (0.20, 0.28), pairedbootstrap, and nDCG diagnostics. Results show the general embedder clearly outper-forms domain BERT, offering a reproducible framework for semantic retrieval undernoisy institutional metadata.
Text embeddings and TLMs/LLMs [1, 2, 3] are regularly implemented to enhance
document retrieval. Pre-trained Legal-BERT [4] contributes to increased performance fordomain-speciﬁc tasks. In case law retrieval, efforts include unsupervised techniques [5]

3.3. Evaluation Metrics and Signiﬁcance
We evaluate ranked retrieval using graded and binary relevance. Each decision is a query,
with neighbours scored by IDF-weighted Jaccard overlap (wJacc) of their keywords.Graded relevance uses this score directly, whereas binary metrics apply two thresholds(0.20 and 0.28). The nDCG@k metric captures both relevance strength and rank position,
remaining τ-independent and robust under noisy labels.
Binary metrics include Precision@k (the share of relevant items among the top k)
and Mean Average Precision (MAP@k ), which reward ranking relevant cases early. Hi-
tRate@k measures the likelihood of retrieving at least one relevant item (“ﬁrst useful
result”), while Rank-Biased Precision (RBP@10) models user patience by emphasizing
early ranks. For diagnostics, WeightedOverlap@k and OverlapCount@k quantify how
many—and how distinctive—keywords are shared between query and retrieved cases,clarifying nDCG trends under diverse label distributions. Statistical signiﬁcance is as-sessed via paired bootstrap resampling over queries, reporting mean differences, 95%conﬁdence intervals, and two-sided p-values.

5. Discussion and Conclusion
Our from-scratch BERT lags behind the off-the-shelf OpenAI embedder. The likely rea-
son is scale and objective: the general embedder beneﬁts from vastly more pretrainingdata and a broader semantic curriculum, yielding representations better aligned for cross-document similarity. In contrast, our domain model is smaller, trained only with MLM,and lacks contrastive or retrieval-aware supervision. Sliding windows (512 with overlap)increase exposure to long texts but add little new signal, as overlapping segments aresemantically redundant and averaging them can dilute discriminative cues. Empirically,the general embedder retrieves neighbors with stronger diagnostic tag overlap even un-der strict thresholds, showing that scale and general semantics dominate domain-onlyMLMs on this task.
Absolute nDCG values represent conservative lower bounds rather than poor utility,
as keyword overlap is a noisy and incomplete gold standard. Despite this, head metrics(P@k, HitRate@k, RBP) and bootstrap tests show large, statistically signiﬁcant robustimprovements for the OpenAI embedder across all cutoffs and thresholds. These resultsindicate that pretraining scale and semantic breadth outweigh domain restriction undernoisy labels. Future work will explore paragraph-level and hybrid sparse–dense retrieval,retrieval-aware pretraining, and expert-based evaluation to better capture legal relevance.

Abstract. Administrative and legal communication is often difﬁcult for laypersons

1. Introduction
Improving the readability of legal and administrative language is vital for access to jus-
tice, as unclear communication can hinder citizens from understanding their rights anderode trust in institutions. This study introduces PONK—an open, modular web applica-tion that combines linguistic and machine-learning methods to evaluate and enhance theclarity of legal texts. PONK assesses how well citizens can understand common admin-istrative documents such as ﬁnes or beneﬁt applications. The Czech Ombudsman’s 2023Annual Report recorded about 7 000 complaints concerning unclear ofﬁcial communi-cation,
2exceeding available assistance. Clearer texts could therefore reduce complaints
and strengthen public trust.
The tool highlights linguistically complex segments and suggests reformulations. Its
backend integrates two modules—lexical surprisal, linguistic rules—combining linguis-
tic analysis with LLM-based semantic assessment. The modular design enables ﬂexible,ﬁne-grained feedback at the sub-sentence level, offering actionable guidance rather thangeneric readability scores. 2. Related Work
Readability reﬂects how easily a text can be processed, while understandability also re-
quires correct interpretation of meaning [1]. Many plain-language metrics applied to le-gal texts overlook these deeper aspects. Automatic formulas based on syntax or vocabu-lary are scalable but correlate weakly with human judgment [2,3], whereas human meth-ods (cloze tests, crowdsourcing) better capture comprehension at higher cost [2,4].
Legal readability research, rooted in the plain-language movement [5], extends to
contracts [6], legislation [7], and legal websites [8]. PONK combines general-languagereadability models with domain-speciﬁc linguistic expertise (Section 4). It integrates twocomplementary approaches: lexical surprisal, which links unexpected words to cognitive
load and reading difﬁculty [9,10,11], and linguistic rules, which evaluate structural and
lexical features such as sentence length, dependency depth, coherence markers, and wordfrequency [12,13,14]. Together, these methods capture both probabilistic and rule-basedsources of legal text complexity.
3. Data
The KUK 0.0 corpus
3was developed speciﬁcally for PONK and serves as the foun-
dation for both modules. It is a pilot collection of Czech legal and administrative texts
designed for the manual and automatic assessment of readability and understandability,with evaluation to follow in later stages.
KUK 0.0 comprises three subcorpora: (1) Public materials of Frank Bold, a non-
proﬁt organization offering plain-language legal guidance for citizens; (2) Statements
of the Ombudsman, opinions addressing speciﬁc complaints from the public (e.g., inasylum or social security matters); and (3) Information ﬂyers of the Ombudsman, brief
educational texts explaining recurring legal issues.
Together, these subcorpora include 6,051 documents and 19.2 million words. KUK
0.0 also incorporates the Czech Court Decisions Corpus (CzCDC 1.0) [15], containingrulings of the Supreme, Supreme Administrative, and Constitutional Courts. The KUK0.0 corpus is unique in classifying Czech legal documents by their degree of understand-ability, enabling both PONK development and its future evaluation on expert and citizen-oriented texts.

4. System Architecture
PONK is a modular client–server application with a web interface and REST API back-
end. The Perl-based core coordinates internal modules and external NLP tools via RESTusing the CoNLL-U format (see Figure 1). External services include UDPipe [16] fortokenization, lemmatization, and syntactic parsing, and NameTag [17] for named entityrecognition. Internally, two modules operate in sequence: the Lexical Surprisal Mod-
ule, which estimates word-level predictability, and the Linguistic Rules Module, which
applies syntax-based readability checks.
The web client allows users to paste or upload text, submit it via REST, and inter-
actively explore results. PONK can also be run as a command-line utility or accessedthrough a public REST API.
4The public instance, available for free non-commercial
use, ensures privacy by not storing processed texts; only minimal metadata (timestamp,data size, conﬁguration, and IP address) is logged, and all external services maintain thesame anonymity policy.
4.1. Lexical Surprisal ModuleLexical surprisal quantiﬁes how unexpected a word is in context, reﬂecting the cognitive
effort required for comprehension [18,19]. High surprisal indicates low readability. Weadapted the GLTR visualization tool [20]—originally designed to detect AI-generatedtext—into Glitter, which highlights word-level surprisal as an indicator of textual difﬁ-
culty.
Input text is tokenized using Czech GPT-2 XL
5,whose 64k-token vocabulary splits
most words into one to three subword units. The model predicts each token from up to128 preceding tokens and computes its probability, producing surprisal scores for everyword. These are color-coded by probability bands, with alternative likely continuationsshown. The visualization helps legal authors spot cognitively demanding segments andrevise them for better readability.
4.2. Linguistic Rules ModuleWe implemented 35 linguistic rules inspired by Czech plain-language handbooks [21,
22,23,24]. These works emphasize clarity, simplicity, and avoidance of ambiguous orcognitively demanding structures. Several rules address the so-called garden-path ef-

All rules are implemented in Python using Udapi6blocks, relying on UDPipe
and NameTag annotations and, where needed, MorphoDiTa [26] for morphological
paradigms. When a parsed subtree matches a rule pattern, relevant tokens are labeled withthe rule name, role-speciﬁc participants, and a unique ID identifying the instance. Rules
are grouped into ﬁve categories for interpretability: ambiguity (10 rules, e.g., garden-
path constructions), clusters (5 rules, frequent patterns lowering readability, e.g., excess
negations), phrases (8 rules, e.g., weak-meaning words), structural (8 rules, e.g., distant
predicates), and acceptability (4 rules, e.g., incomplete conjunctions).
In the interface, each category is visualized with distinct highlight colors, with grey
marking overlaps. Current limitations include the inability to process larger textual unitsbeyond sentences and the lack of deeper lexical-semantic understanding—factors thatrestrict the precision of some cluster and semantic rules.
5. Evaluation
5.1. Evaluation of Lexical Surprisal ModuleWe qualitatively evaluated the lexical surprisal module on 50 randomly selected docu-
ments from the KUK 0.0 corpus, using its visual interface where word surprisal is color-coded from blue (low) to red (high). The analysis, conducted by legal and linguistic ex-perts in our team, focused on how these gradients correspond to perceived readability(see Figure 2). Although exploratory, the evaluation provided useful insights into inter-pretability and model behavior.
Low-surprisal words (dark blue) often appear in ﬁxed expressions, indicating ﬂuency
but sometimes redundancy, while high-surprisal words (red) frequently disrupt sentenceﬂow. Surprisal naturally decreases as the context lengthens. Similar to [20], we observedthat a balanced mix of predictable and unexpected words produces natural, comprehen-sible text, whereas excessive unpredictability reduces clarity. Contrary to expectations,specialized legal terms often received low surprisal—language models predict them eas-ily due to their presence in large training corpora. Future work will adapt promptingstrategies to better reﬂect lay comprehensibility while retaining contextual accuracy.
5.2. Evaluation of Linguistic Rules ModuleWe evaluated the linguistic rules on 30 texts from the KUK 0.0 corpus, including Om-
budsman materials and court decisions from the ConCo and SupAdmCo subcorpora ofCzCDC 1.0 (see Section 3). The rules were applied and visually inspected using the BratRapid Annotation Tool.

6. Conclusion and Future Work
PONK integrates two complementary methods—lexical surprisal and linguistically in-
formed rules—enhanced by expert knowledge of Czech legal drafting (see Section 4).These modules provide real-time feedback at the word level, effectively identifying un-clear passages. Qualitative evaluation conﬁrmed their usefulness, though broader testingon larger datasets is needed.
Future work will compare surprisal patterns in original and simpliﬁed legal texts, re-
ﬁne rule thresholds through genre-speciﬁc proﬁles, and explore multiple language mod-els for surprisal estimation. A planned third, supervised module will assess textual co-herence and relevance, extending PONK toward deeper semantic evaluation. Its modulararchitecture enables seamless integration of such advances, ensuring ongoing alignmentwith research in legal readability.

EmoLawConnect: An AI-Powered
Kohei OSHIOa,1
aGraduate School of Information and Communication, Meiji University, Japan
Abstract. EmoLawConnect is an AI-powered matching engine for family conﬂict
resolution that recommends lawyers by combining legal case proﬁles with clients’
emotional preferences and value alignment. It integrates a multi-layer pipeline thatprocesses user inputs (e.g., emotional expression, legal needs) and professional pro-ﬁles (e.g., legal expertise, practice orientation). The architecture merges rule-basedpre-ﬁltering with a semantic–emotional scoring module built on matrix factoriza-tion and value-aware alignment. The prototype was evaluated through scenario-based testing and a rule-based legal-consistency proxy. Results suggest improveduser–professional compatibility and trust, with potential contributions to access tojustice. The approach provides a foundation for broader legal-service applicationswhere affective or interpersonal alignment matters.
Keywords. AI and law, legal tech, professional matching, access to justice, family
dispute resolution, value alignment
1. Introduction
Access to legal professionals in family-related conﬂicts (e.g., divorce, custody, inheri-
tance) requires not only legal expertise but also sensitivity to emotional and relationaldynamics. Existing legal tech often focuses on document automation or rule-based guid-ance, yet rarely considers interpersonal compatibility between users and professionals,which can materially affect negotiation outcomes.
Building on our prior work on a negotiation-support chatbot that estimates both
Legal-Emotional BATNA [1], and on follow-up interviews with former judges and prac-ticing attorneys in Japanese family law, we emphasize the need for detailed user proﬁling.Relevant attributes include family structure, marital history, conﬂict patterns, personalitytraits, and communication styles [2,3].
To comply with Article 72 of Japan’s Attorney Act, EmoLawConnect (i) does not
provide legal advice, (ii) does not broker legal services for compensation, and (iii)presents outputs as internal decision support for licensed professionals. UI ﬂows and con-tractual terms ensure that ﬁnal client-engagement decisions remain solely with attorneysand law ﬁrms.

This paper details the system architecture, matching algorithm design, and a pre-
liminary evaluation framework for EmoLawConnect. The current prototype focuses on
rule-based matching using structured user and expert proﬁles. Future work includes
human-in-the-loop validation with domain experts, calibration analysis, and evaluationon anonymized real-world datasets within existing referral workﬂows.Contributions. (i) a rule-isolated proxy for legal consistency, (ii) an affect/value diag-
nostic kept out of supervision, and (iii) a compact neural scorer that outperforms MF onthe proxy task.
2. Related Work
Recommender systems infer user preferences from behavioral traces across domains
such as e-commerce, media, and healthcare. Legal settings pose distinct challenges: mat-ters are sensitive, intents vary widely, and professional proﬁles are heterogeneous. Earlylegal recommenders relied on ontology-based matching between user problems and legalknowledge, prioritizing explainability over personalization [4].
Data-driven approaches later modeled implicit compatibility via collaborative ﬁlter-
ing (CF); matrix factorization (MF) projects users and professionals into a shared la-tent space to capture afﬁnities [7]. Incorporating side information, proﬁles, and contextimproves over pure CF [6]. Surveys codify evaluation protocols and ranking metrics[14,18], while MNAR biases warn against na ¨ıve train/test designs [17].
In emotionally charged domains (e.g., family law), behavioral traces alone are insuf-
ﬁcient. Affective/personality-aware recommenders suggest that value/affect congruenceboosts satisfaction and trust [16,19]. Legal-tech for vulnerable users highlights the needfor empathic, careful UX [5].
Beyond accuracy, high-stakes contexts require attention to ethics and process.
Fairness-aware recommendation studies exposure/representation via constraints and re-ranking [9,10,11]; work on interpretability and legitimacy cautions against na ¨ıve trans-
parency [12,8,13].
We also connect to legal-aid triage and referral systems reporting operational con-
straints in intake, eligibility, and routing; our intake minimalism borrows from these de-ployments while adding an affect-aware diagnostic layer [20,21,22,23,24].
EmoLawConnect contributes at this intersection by: (i) combining legal specializa-
tion with affective–value signals; (ii) treating the Emotional-Aware Alignment Score(EAS) as a diagnostic (not supervisory) signal within the evaluation pipeline; and
(iii) aligning optimization with legal practice by evaluating against a rule-based legal-consistency proxy instead of an expert gold set, thereby isolating legal constraints fromaffective alignment in the current prototype.

6. Discussion
The results suggest that EmoLawConnect can rank suitable professionals well under a
rule-based legal proxy, while EAS provides an interpretable signal of affective ﬁt. Gains
on Precision@5, NDCG, and ROC AUC indicate that combining structured proﬁles witha lightweight neural scorer is effective; EAS is informative diagnostically but is keptoutside supervision to avoid leakage.
Limitations remain. The synthetic dataset cannot capture the full social and interper-
sonal context of family law. Fixed-length affect/value vectors simplify dynamic states.K. Oshio / EmoLawConnect 340

Future evaluations should combine expert review, small-signal ﬁeld studies within refer-
ral workﬂows, and calibration analysis.
Architecture-wise, the system is modular. A justiﬁcation module can generate short
natural-language rationales from dialogue and metadata, and these rationales can be em-bedded and fed back to the scorer as an auxiliary feature. The same modularity extendsto many-to-many settings (e.g., lawyer–counselor–mediator teams) by scoring candidateteams with both legal constraints and average EAS, then optimizing under workload anddiversity constraints.
Ethically, deployment must prioritize procedural legitimacy: fairness-aware expo-
sure, transparent operating points, and user-facing explanations proportionate to risk[8,9,10,11]. These concerns are integral to design, not an afterthought.
Data collection in referral workﬂows is constrained: users and professionals provide
sparse, strategic, and sometimes inconsistent inputs. We therefore scope the supervisedtarget to a legal proxy and treat affective alignment as diagnostic, while designing theintake to minimize burden (≤10 items, defaultable answers) and mirror existing referralforms.
As a next step, we will run a pilot (≈15–20 cases) inside an existing referral work-
ﬂow, collecting user-reported satisfaction, perceived ﬁt, 7-day intent-to-retain, expertagreement (Cohen’s κ), and proxy agreement (AUC/NDCG).
7. Conclusion and Future Work
We presented EmoLawConnect, a matching engine for family-law services that pairs
legal relevance with affect/value considerations. Under a rule-based legal proxy, a simple
MLP over structured proﬁles outperformed an MF baseline, and EAS offered a usefuldiagnostic of interpersonal ﬁt.
Next steps focus on realism and governance: (i) expert-reviewed and user-involved
evaluations with anonymized real cases, (ii) calibration and robustness checks, (iii) mul-timodal proﬁling that augments surveys with text-derived embeddings, and (iv) teammatching with fairness and workload constraints. The goal is not to automate legal judg-ment, but to improve human–human matching in emotionally complex settings whilerespecting legal and ethical boundaries.

Defending the Hierarchical Result Models
of Precedential Constraint
Henry PRAKKENa,1and Wijnand V AN WOERKOMb
aDepartment of Information and Computing Sciences, Utrecht University,
Utrecht, The Netherlands
bMax Planck Institute for Comparative and International Private Law,
Hamburg, Germany
Abstract. In recent years, hierarchical case-based-reasoning models of precedential
constraint have been proposed. Trevor Bench-Capon criticised these models, among
other things, on the grounds that they would not account for the possibility that
intermediate factors are established with different strengths by different base-level
factors. In this paper we respond to these criticisms for van Woerkom’s result-
based hierarchical models. We argue that in some examples Bench-Capon seems
to interpret intermediate factors as dimensions, and that applying van Woerkom’s
dimension-based version of the hierarchical result model to these examples avoids
Bench-Capon’s criticisms.
Keywords. case-based reasoning, precedential constraint, intermediate factors
1. Introduction
In [7] a hierarchical factor-based model of precedential constraint was proposed, extending
the ‘ﬂat’ factor-based result and reason models of precedential constraint of [ 5]. V ery
brieﬂy, the ﬂat model represents cases as a binary decision plus a fact situation, which
consists of two sets of factors pro and con the decision. A decision in a new fact situation
isforced if a precedent for that decision exists that cannot be distinguished from the new
fact situation, i.e., if the latter contains at least all pro-decision factors of the precedent
and at most all con-decision factors of the precedent. In [ 7] this is reﬁned in terms of a
factor hierarchy [ 1], in which basic factors are pro or con more abstract factors, which
ultimately are pro or con the ﬁnal binary decision. This allows to make the forcedness of
the ﬁnal decision relative to intermediate decisions instead of to basic factors.
In [2,3], Trevor Bench-Capon criticised the resulting model, among other things,
on the ground that it does not account for the possibility that intermediate factors are
established with different strengths by different base-level factors. In this paper we argue
that in some examples Bench-Capon seems to interpret intermediate factors as dimensions,
and that applying [ 6]’s dimension-based version of the hierarchical result model to these
examples avoids Bench-Capon’s criticisms.

Jo with two children Emma and Max, where the parents want to consistently decide about
whether their children can have ice cream. Bench-Capon assumes the factor hierarchy

that Max could have his ice cream. Bench-Capon says that in a hierarchical model of
precedential constraint there are two possible interpretations of this case.
•MMH: Q>R(behaving at home is more important than behaving at school)
•MMF: F1>F5(folding one’s clothes is more important than being inattentive in

Note that MMH and MMF correspond to the hierarchical and ﬂat constraint model

these two interpretations is not obvious. It is worthwhile quoting him in full:
Jo may give clues as to her interpretation. If she says ok, you tidied your room, which
meant you behaved at home, so you can have ice cream even though you misbehaved
at school, she is clearly thinking in hierarchical terms. If, on the other hand she says ok,
you folded your clothes so you can have ice cream even though you were inattentive
in class, she is clearly thinking in terms of MMF.

hierarchy is given in a way in which all base-level factors establish intermediate factors
with the same strength, then there is nothing wrong with MMH. Bench-Capon’s intuition
can then be explained by noting that intermediate factors are not always established with
the same strength. This becomes clear from his discussion of another example.

5. Conclusion
In this paper we have responded to Trevor Bench-Capon’s criticism in [ 2,3] of hierarchical
result models of precedential constraint. We have argued that his point that the models
do not account for the possibility that intermediate factors are established with different
strengths by different base-level factors does not apply to [ 6]’s dimension-based version.
We have shown that in the analysis of some examples Bench-Capon seems to interpret
some intermediate factors as dimensions, and that applying [ 6]’s hierarchical result model
to these examples avoids Bench-Capon’s criticisms.References

Abstract. The increasing availability of legal documentation provides opportuni-
ties for applying empirical research methods that enable a comprehensive analysis
of complex legal data. Systematic Content Analysis offers a structured approachfor examining legal texts. This paper examines the possibility of anomaly detectionin legal text through the employment of machine learning methods. The conclu-sions presented are formulated on a basis of a case study focusing on contractualagreements concluded between public authorities and private service providers inthe ﬁeld of cybersecurity. In this regard, we propose an approach to the detectionof anomalous legal text, providing a categorization of attributes that impact the de-termination of anomalies and describing their signiﬁcance in the selected domain.
Keywords. systematic content analysis, machine learning, anomaly detection, legal
text, cybersecurity
1. Introduction
Legal research focuses, primarily, on the examination of different legal documentation
(legislation, case law, contractual agreements, etc.), drawing conclusions from its thor-ough reading and interpretation. The increasing availability of legal text provides oppor-tunities for researchers to implement different empirical research methods enabling com-prehensive analysis of complex legal data. Systematic content analysis provides a basisfor such analysis, facilitating efﬁcient examination of textual information in a standard-ized manner and application of different machine learning methods in this regard.
The main objective of this paper is the analysis of anomaly detection in legal texts.
One of the important tasks in machine learning is the identiﬁcation of anomalies (out-
liers), and in this study we examine how this concept can be applied to contracts.Anomaly detection refers to the problem of ﬁnding patterns in data that do not conform

to expected behaviour, identifying signiﬁcant (and often critical) actionable information
in a wide variety of application domains [1]. To achieve this objective, we deﬁne thefollowing partial research questions: (1) What constitutes an anomaly in legal texts?;(2) Which attributes contribute to anomalous contracts, and which characterize standard(non-anomalous) agreements?
To answer these questions, we focus on unsupervised outlier detection methods ap-
plied to legal contracts in the ﬁeld of cybersecurity. The dataset consists of contracts
whose subject matter is the provision of various cybersecurity-related services. In paral-lel, we apply Systematic Content Analysis (SCA), which represents a structured em-
pirical approach for analyzing legal texts. This dual perspective—combining outlier de-tection techniques with SCA allows us to identify anomalous contracts, explore attributecategories inﬂuencing their classiﬁcation, and distinguish between standard contractualfeatures and those contributing to anomalies.
The increasing employment of empirical research methods, including SCA in legal
research has been discussed in numerous studies [2,3,4]. Another research group focusesonthe detection of anomalies in the judicial system and legal texts [5,6]. The detec-
tion of anomalies in legal texts is closely related not only to the application of law butalso to the legislative process. In [7], the authors focused on improving the quality oflegislation and legal decisions through knowledge veriﬁcation and anomaly detection.
2. Methodology
From a methodological point of view, this paper employs the SCA, which can be deﬁned
as a methodical, replicable technique for compressing many words of text into fewercontent categories based on explicit coding rules [8]. The advantage of this approach isthat it can produce both qualitative and quantitative results by enabling the researcher tocompress long text into fewer content categories based on explicit rules of coding [9].
The analysis is based on a dataset of contracts obtained from the Slovak Central
Register of Contracts – a public database of contracts obligatorily published pursuantto the Act No. 211/2000 Coll. on free access to information. The authors have analysed273 contracts concluded in the time period 23.7.2019 – 1.1.2025, and used types of at-tributes, namely numerical (e.g., the amount of remuneration), and binary (e.g., inclusionof a contractual ﬁne). Binary attributes represent the occurrence or the absence of a spe-ciﬁc attribute. The analysis resulted in the selection and collection of a set of attributesclassiﬁed into the six groups.
For anomaly detection we used LSCP [10] (Locally Selective Combination in Par-
allel), a dynamic ensemble that, for each sample, (1) ﬁnds a small local neighborhood(via k-nearest neighbors), (2) builds a simple pseudo-target for that neighborhood, (3)measures each base detector’s competency as its correlation with that pseudo-target, and(4) averages the scores of only the most competent detectors for that sample. We en-semble six unsupervised detectors — PCA [11], ECOD [12], COPOD [13], Isolation-
Forest [14], HBOS [15], and KNN [16]. For each sample, LSCP builds a k-NN neigh-
borhood, forms a simple pseudo-target from neighbors’ consensus, and measures eachdetector’s competency as its correlation with that pseudo-target. These correlations arediscretized into 4 bins; We set contamination to 0.05 as a standard unsupervised.
For the purpose of analyzing attributes and their impact on the anomaly of legal texts,
we employed the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) [17] method. We explain LSCPP . Sokol et al. / Anomaly Detection in Legal Text – A Case Study on Cybersecurity Contracts 351

anomaly scores with SamplingSHAP—a faster alternative to KernelSHAP that preserves
reliable feature-importance rankings. SHAP compares each prediction to a baseline (the
model’s expected output on typical cases), so we use a compact background of 30 k-means centroids to represent those cases.
3. Results and discussions
After running SamplingSHAP on the LSCP trained model, we obtained per-feature at-
tributions that can be visualized in the beeswarm plot (Figure 1). This plot shows how
all attributes contribute across the dataset, highlighting which features consistently driveanomaly detection. This explanation allows us not only to detect outliers but also to un-derstand the underlying reasons for their anomalous character.

3.2. Discussion regarding contracts
As part of the discussion, we focused on a speciﬁc contract that exhibits the highest
anomaly (with ID 5821279), and a contract (with ID 6332291) that can be consideredstandard. According to statistical data obtained from the processing of selected contrac-tual attributes, the agreement exhibiting the highest level (ID 5821279) of anomalies de-viating from the norm (–0.17) concerns the provider’s obligation to deliver consultancyservices to the contracting authority in the areas of information security, cybersecurity,personal data protection, and IT service management. The contract shows the greatestdegree of deviation among the examined attributes with respect to the imposition of apenalty on a public administration entity for delayed payment (+0.49), the delivery ofincomplete documentation (+0.37), and the limitation of liability for damages (+0.3).Within the contractual framework established between the parties, the service provideris entitled, though not obliged, to claim payment of a contractual penalty amounting to0.5% of the outstanding sum for each day of delay. Ordinarily, late payment is sanctionedby statutory or contractual default interest. The contracting parties further agreed on alimitation of liability for damages capped at the price for a “chosen period.” However,the contract does not explicitly deﬁne what constitutes such a period. The total contrac-tual price to be paid to the provider amounts to EUR 154,800, which simultaneouslyrepresents the notional ceiling of liability for damages expressed in pecuniary terms.
In contrast, the contract with the lowest level (ID 5821279) of anomalies (-0.17)
refers to the consultation on cybersecurity measures and the supervision of the oper-ator’s cybersecurity and its cybersecurity manager. The least deviating attributes arethe turnover criterion (–0.15), deﬁnition of material breach (–0.14), and conﬁdentialityclauses (–0.12). The contract generally sets out grounds for withdrawal and requires bothparties to protect conﬁdential information as they would their own, promptly report anyunauthorised use or disclosure, and cooperate in restoring its protection.
4. Conclusion
In this paper, we demonstrated a possible approach to the examination and identiﬁcation
of anomalies within the scope of SCA of legal text, focusing on contractual agreementsconcluded in cybersecurity as our case study. The proposed approach may ﬁnd its appli-cation in relation to other legal text with the objective of identifying the established legalpractice and possible deviations from it. The examined attributes focused on standardaspects of contractual agreements regarding their subject matter, liability, conﬁdentiality,etc. In this regard, we calculated the impact of individual attributes on the classiﬁcationof contracts as anomalous and provided their categorization into different categories, re-ﬂecting their relevance for anomaly detection. The presence of certain attributes in legaltext aided in its classiﬁcation as anomalous, or, correspondingly, determined the ‘stan-dard’ formulation of contractual provisions in the examined case study.

Abstract. Legal and administrative sources typically describe procedural steps that
are not recorded in structured data, which makes the application of process-oriented
analysis particularly challenging. In this work, we present an approach that usesLarge Language Models (LLMs) to extract events and dates from unstructured le-gal texts. The methodology is applied to a dataset of Italian procurement noticespublished since 2022 on the ofﬁcial EU platform, Tenders Electronic Daily (TED),demonstrating how LLMs can extract valuable information, such as administrativedecisions adopted prior to tender publication. These elements are incorporated intoexisting event logs, thereby enhancing the quality of process analysis. A sampleof the extracted data has been manually reviewed by legal experts to assess therelevance and correctness of the automated detection. The results suggest that thisapproach can help identify procedural steps hidden in free text, thereby supportingmore complete and accurate representations of legal workﬂows.
Keywords. Legal Process Analysis, Event Log Enrichment, Textual Analysis in
Procurement
1. Introduction
The growing availability of digital data has increased attention to legal research [3]. Le-
gal and administrative procedures, such as public procurement, are documented throughlegislation, notices, and rulings, yet critical process information remains in unstructuredtext. While information systems record standardised events, relevant procedural detailsoften appear only in free-text sections, hindering automated analysis.
This research applies Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language
Models (LLMs) [25] to extract events and dates from procurement notices on the EU

Our contributions are: (i) a pipeline leveraging LLMs for extracting information

Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3presents methodology; Section 4 describes the dataset; Section 5 presents results; Sec-tion 6 concludes describing the future work.
2. Related Work
The automated analysis of legal procedures can be approached through business pro-
cess management (BPM) [12] and, in particular, process mining (PM) [36], which re-constructs workﬂows from event logs to identify bottlenecks [29,30], assess compli-ance [31], and optimise resources [27]. However, structured event data are rarely avail-able in legal contexts [14], where procedural information often resides in textual sourcessuch as regulations, rulings, or administrative documents [22]. Early computational mod-els aimed to capture the normative structure of legal processes [15], while more recenthybrid approaches combine structured data and text to improve completeness [8,26].
Information extraction has long supported the creation of legal knowledge bases
through rule-based and machine learning techniques [18]. Various NLP methods havebeen applied to Named Entity Recognition in legal documents [2], from early statisticalmodels [11] to domain-speciﬁc corpora for Indian [17], English [4], and German [20]legal texts. Yet, these methods remain sensitive to domain variability and linguistic am-biguity.
The advent of LLMs has brought advances in summarisation, question answer-
ing [28], and event extraction [19]. In the legal domain, LLMs have been explored forjudgment prediction [37], contract analysis [32], legal summarisation [10], harmonisa-tion [5,6], and entity–relation extraction [21]. Despite these successes, concerns aboutbias and explainability highlight the need for expert supervision [9].
Building on our earlier work [35,27], which introduced a process-oriented frame-
work for event extraction from tender notices, this study extends that approach with atwo-stage expert-based validation strategy, achieving higher accuracy on a larger dataset.
3. Methodological Framework
This section outlines the methodological framework for identifying relevant events
within legal documents. Our approach integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) withexpert validation to extract structured data from unstructured legal texts. The frameworkconsists of two main stages — extraction and evaluation — supported by iterative expertfeedback, as shown in Figure 1.I. Spada et al. / An Expert-Validated LLM Framework 357

Overview. The two-stage methodology (Figure 1) combines prompt-based event ex-
traction with legal expert evaluation. Each stage includes an extraction phase — from
prompt engineering to machine-readable linking — followed by manual expert assess-ment of accuracy and completeness. Two legal experts participated in the evaluation toensure compliance with domain standards.
