Preliminary Inspection. An exploratory phase was conducted with domain experts,
building on previous ﬁndings [35]. This phase reﬁned the requirements and prompts byanalysing a sample of legal documents and updating the extraction guidelines. Keywordand abbreviation ﬁltering improved document selection (e.g., DL, DM, LR, DGR), en-suring that only notices likely to contain relevant event–date pairs were included. Col-laboration between legal experts and computer scientists deﬁned both domain-speciﬁcrequirements and evaluation criteria, ensuring methodological consistency.
Stage 1. The assessment stage compared multiple prompting strategies across differ-
ent LLMs to assess: (i) zero-shot, (ii) few-shot, and (iii) chain-of-thought (CoT) ap-
proaches. Manual evaluation of a subset of the dataset identiﬁed the best-performingmodel–prompt combination according to expert guidelines, enabling selection of the op-timal conﬁguration for large-scale testing.
Stage 2. In the experiment stage, the selected conﬁguration was applied to a repre-
sentative sample of TED documents. Multiple experts independently annotated the re-
sults, and inter-annotator agreement was measured using Cohen’s κ[7]. This validation
conﬁrmed the reliability and domain validity of the extracted data.
4. From Methodology to Practice: The Case Study
This section presents the case study and its application of the proposed framework. The
study analyses 27,841 Italian public procurement notices published on TED in 2022 [13].The year 2022 was chosen because it followed the pandemic period and allowed com-pleted procedures to be observed. While some sections of the notices follow a structuredtemplate with standardised ﬁelds, others contain free-text descriptions of procedural acts.In particular, the sections titled “complementary information” or “additional informa-tion” often include decrees and decisions marking the start of procurement procedures,which are the focus of this study.I. Preliminary inspection. Following our framework, we conducted an exploratory anal-

5. Results
V alidation of the ﬁrst extraction results. The ﬁrst extraction was evaluated by two in-
dependent annotators using a three-label scheme (Yes, No, Doubts). The overall agree-
ment reached a Cohen’s κof 0.576, which corresponds to a moderate level of inter-
annotator reliability. This outcome suggests that, while the LLM-generated results aregenerally consistent, the presence of the Doubts category introduced some ambiguityinto the annotation process, reﬂecting borderline or less clear-cut cases. After discussingand resolving the doubtful cases, the two legal experts proposed a ﬁnal assessment ofthe events and dates correctly extracted by the LLM. Speciﬁcally, out of 121 cases, 89answers were correct (74%), while the model was incorrect in 32 cases (24%). This out-come is unsatisfactory, thereby justifying a second annotation with a new prompt and asubset of notices to increase the percentage of successful cases.
Improved annotation guidelines. The two-stage annotation process enhanced guide-
line accuracy through iterative reﬁnement and identiﬁcation of previously undetected
edge cases. Legal experts revised the annotation scheme from tripartite (“Yes/No/Doubt”)to binary (“Yes/No”) classiﬁcation. This simpliﬁcation eliminated the “doubt” category,which introduced unnecessary uncertainty without discriminative value. Establishingstricter, more explicit decision criteria from the outset reduced annotator uncertaintyand improved inter-annotator agreement. Additionally, the target term set was expanded

Expert guidance enabled prompt reﬁnement by selectively ﬁltering concept quali-

Assessment of strategies. The system prompt incorporates legal expert analysis of pre-
liminary TED instances, specifying the extraction task, relevant keywords with abbre-

Three prompting strategies were evaluated. The zero-shot prompt (Prompt 1) pro-
vides a baseline that incorporates four expert-deﬁned requirements, requesting JSONoutput with the “event” and “date” ﬁelds. The few-shot prompt (Prompt 2) extends thisby adding three practical examples. The CoT prompt (Prompt 3) introduces explicit step-by-step reasoning for entity extraction in the process mining context, including a demon-stration.
Manual evaluation on 10 randomly selected instances compared the three strategies
across models with varying characteristics: Claude-Sonnet-4 (Prompt 1: 8; Prompt 2: 7;
Prompt 3: 9),GPT-4o (Prompt 1: 7; Prompt 2: 7; Prompt 3: 8), Llama-3.1-8B (Prompt 1:
2; Prompt 2: 6; Prompt 3: 4). The optimal conﬁguration was Claude-Sonnet-4 with CoT.
V alidation of second extraction results. Inter-annotator agreement between two legal

The model correctly identiﬁed 108 of 115 cases (94%), with 7 errors (6%), demonstrat-

6. Conclusion and Future Work
This work presents a two-stage framework for extracting legally meaningful events and
dates from administrative texts. Applied to large-scale procurement data, it enables theidentiﬁcation of information useful for assessing public administrations’ performanceand provides an empirical basis for transparency and accountability analyses. From alegal perspective, the method also helps address systemic issues such as limited trans-parency and corruption. During evaluation, the LLM showed a partial ability to distin-guish relevant from irrelevant information—correctly ignoring non-pertinent decrees orresolutions in several cases—while still struggling with more subtle distinctions, such asthose between resolutions initiating or annulling a procedure.
A key insight is that legal meaning depends on institutional context and procedural
relevance rather than on isolated terms. By incorporating expert validation, the approachdemonstrates that legal knowledge is essential for guiding computational analysis andproducing data-driven evaluations of procurement processes.

Label Indeterminacy in AI & Law
Cor STEGINGaTadeusz ZBIEGIE ´Nb
aBernoulli Institute of Mathematics, Computer Science and Artiﬁcial Intelligence,
University of Groningen
bDepartment of Legal Theory, Jagiellonian University
Abstract. Machine learning is increasingly used in the legal domain, typically op-
erating retrospectively by treating past case outcomes as ground truth. However,
legal outcomes are often shaped by human interventions that are not captured in
most machine learning approaches. A ﬁnal decision may result from a settlement,
an appeal, or other procedural actions. This creates label indeterminacy: the out-
come could have been different if the intervention had or had not taken place. We
argue that legal machine learning applications need to account for label indetermi-nacy. Methods to impute indeterminate labels exist, but are all grounded in unveri-
ﬁable assumptions. In the context of classifying cases from the European Court of
Human Rights, we show that the way that labels are constructed during training cansigniﬁcantly affect model behaviour. We therefore position label indeterminacy as
a relevant concern in AI & Law and demonstrate how it can shape model behaviour.
Keywords. Label indeterminacy, machine learning, legal decision-making
1. Introduction
With recent advances in machine learning, AI is increasingly applied in law, yet many
approaches remain ill-suited for legal tasks. Limitations include the retrospective natureof machine learning, lack of faithful explanations [1,2], and, in generative models, issuessuch as hallucinations [3]. One crucial machine learning issue that has not yet been ex-plored in the legal domain is label indeterminacy [4], where the labels of certain train-
ing instances are inherently unknown because an intervention by a decision maker hasaffected the ﬁnal outcome. For example, in medicine, if life-sustaining treatment is with-held, it is impossible to know whether the patient would have survived if treated [5]. Theresulting selectively labelled data can strongly inﬂuence model behaviour [4].
Many analogous scenarios exist in law, including bail decisions, settlements, and ap-
peals. When bail is denied, we cannot know whether the defendant would have appeared
in court if released. Similarly, if a case is settled or not appealed, the outcome that wouldhave resulted from litigation or an appeal remains unknown. Accounting for these inde-terminate labels is vital. In this paper, we examine the legal task of court case prediction.We investigate when and why decisions in non-appealed cases should be treated as inde-terminate rather than ground truth, and review methods for imputing these labels. UsingEuropean Court of Human Rights case data, we show that commonly applied strategiesfor handling label indeterminacy can lead to substantially different model predictions.

2. Background
Machine learning approaches to automated legal prediction constitute an established sub-
ﬁeld, with various models attempting to classify case outcomes across different legal do-mains [6,7,8,9,10]. Most prior research treats past case outcomes as ﬁxed labels, assum-ing the ﬁnal judgement unambiguously resolves the dispute [11,12]. This assumption isproblematic under label indeterminacy, where outcomes may depend on interventionssuch as appeals, settlements, or other procedural decisions.
Label indeterminacy differs from selection bias, which arises when datasets capture
only a non-representative slice of disputes [13]. Excluding settled cases would produce
selection bias, while including them creates indeterminate labels, as the true court out-come is unknowable. Thus, a ‘ﬁnal judgement’ in a dataset may not fully reﬂect theunderlying dispute.
Label indeterminacy is also distinct from jurisprudential legal indeterminacy, a de-
bate arising from realist critiques of formalism [14,15]. It argues that legal reasoning maynot yield a single inevitable answer because rules are underdetermined [16,17]. Critical
legal studies scholars add that outcomes are shaped by power dynamics rather than rule-following [17,18]. Dworkin [19] rebutted this, arguing that even hard cases have a right‘answer’ discoverable through proper interpretation. More broadly, the notion of ‘truth’in law is often socially and institutionally constituted: Patterson challenges the corre-spondence view, locating truth in accepted argumentative forms [20,21,22], an approachalso recognized in AI & Law research [23,24,25].
While we do not settle theoretical disputes, these perspectives support viewing legal
outcomes as contingent, procedural, and context-dependent. Treating all labels as ﬁxed
ground truths risks misrepresenting the phenomena machine learning models seek to cap-ture. Our experiments show that how indeterminate labels are handled can substantially
affect model behaviour, which may reinforce historical biases and ultimately undermine
the reliability of AI applications in law.
3. European Court of Human Rights
We investigate label indeterminacy in the domain of the European Court of Human
Rights (ECtHR), where we develop a machine learning model to predict case outcomes.
The ECtHR hears most cases in a seven-judge Chamber, decided by majority vote [26]. Insome cases, either on referral or after relinquishment, the case proceeds to the seventeen-judge Grand Chamber, whose judgment is ﬁnal. Referral is discretionary; many Cham-ber judgments stand without review. This raises a modelling question: if a case is not re-ferred, should the Chamber judgment be treated as deﬁnitive? Legally, Chamber rulingsare binding unless overturned, yet they lack the authority of Grand Chamber judgments.From a machine learning perspective, we cannot model both simultaneously, as their de-cisions can conﬂict, for example, when a case is appealed and overturned by the GrandChamber.
In this study, we treat Grand Chamber judgments as ground truth and regard Cham-
ber outcomes as indeterminate. This framework allows us to investigate how differentstrategies for handling label indeterminacy, such as treating Chamber decisions as provi-sional or excluding them entirely, affect classiﬁer behaviour. 6. Discussion
In this experiment, chamber case outcomes are considered indeterminate, so we cannot
judge the correctness of predictions on these cases. Furthermore, all nine label imputa-tion methods rely on unveriﬁable assumptions (Table 1) and none can be regarded as ab-solutely ‘correct’. They were chosen from the literature to illustrate label indeterminacyin law, even if some assumptions may be especially implausible in legal contexts.
Figure 1 shows that predictive behaviour varies by imputation method: ex p

lights two example cases, where predictions range up to 0.91 across methods. Examiningthe two cases revealed no clear reason for the divergent predictions. Both are Chambercases, one with a single dissent and the other decided by majority, suggesting that ordi-nary cases such as these can be strongly affected by how label indeterminacy is handled.
Our results highlight the importance of accounting for label indeterminacy, as the
choice of method can substantially affect model behaviour. Predicting ECtHR case out-comes is challenging even for humans [32], and serves mainly as an academic illus-tration and illustrative case study. Similar issues arise in other legal contexts, such assettlements, withdrawals, procedural defaults, bail, or appeals.
7. Conclusion
We introduce the concept of label indeterminacy to the legal domain and highlight its crit-
ical implications for machine learning. Certain legal outcomes are inherently unknow-able because they depend on interventions whose absence or alteration could have pro-duced different results. This creates indeterminate labels that cannot be ignored in pre-dictive modeling. Using the ECtHR as a case study, we show that commonly applied la-bel imputation strategies can yield different prediction behaviours, emphasizing the needto explicitly address indeterminacy when designing and evaluating AI systems in law.

From Court Decisions to Guiding
Principles: Advancing Complex Legal
Summarization with LLMs
May Myo ZINa,1,Ken SA TOHaand Georg BORGESb
aCenter for Juris-Informatics, ROIS-DS, T okyo, Japan
bInstitute of Legal Informatics, Saarland University, Saarbr ¨ucken, Germany
Abstract. Guiding principles (Leits ¨atze) are central to German jurisprudence, cap-
turing the essence of judicial reasoning in concise, doctrinally precise statements.
Unlike general case summaries, they distill normative reasoning and key legal hold-ings rather than recounting factual backgrounds or procedural details. This paperexamines how large language models (LLMs) can automatically generate guid-ing principles from German court decisions, focusing on three dimensions: modelchoice and adaptation, prompting strategies, and evaluation methods. ComparingGPT-4o with LerLeoLM, a ﬁne-tuned, domain-speciﬁc model, we ﬁnd that GPT-4ooutperforms even without ﬁne-tuning, while lightweight tuning on only 100 casesyields the best results. Human–LLM co-designed prompts further enhance quality,surpassing both expert-structured and self-generated prompts. Finally, we show thatLLM-based evaluation aligns more closely with expert judgment than traditionalmetrics, establishing guiding principle generation as a distinct task in Legal NLP .
Keywords. large language models, guiding principles, German court decisions,
prompt engineering, legal summarization, LLM-based evaluation
1. Introduction
Automatically generating guiding principles is a unique challenge, as it requires domain-
speciﬁc abstraction, conciseness, and legal precision that go beyond the abilities of stan-dard summarization methods, which tend to reproduce factual details or yield vague gen-eralities. Recent large language models (LLMs) show promise in legal reasoning [1] andjudgment summarization [2,3,4], but their effectiveness in generating guiding principlesremains underexplored. This study investigates the use of LLMs to generate guidingprinciples from German court decisions. We address three core research questions:
1.RQ1: Can zero-shot prompting using advanced proprietary LLMs like GPT-4o
rival or even surpass domain-speciﬁc models ﬁne-tuned for this task?
2.RQ2: How much does expert-crafted prompting matter when models already
possess strong prior knowledge of the task?
3.RQ3: Are conventional evaluation metrics sufﬁcient for guiding principle gener-
ation, or is LLM-based evaluation better aligned with expert evaluation?

2. Related Work
Most research on applying LLMs to legal judgments centers on summarization tasks
[6,7,8,9,16,17]. Sharma and Singh [12] used InLegalBERT [13] embeddings with K-Means clustering for extractive summarization, outperforming Legal Pegasus, T5, BART,and ChatGPT-3.5, though producing case-like summaries. Glaser et al. [14] introduceda dataset of German rulings with abstractive summaries, focusing on summarizationrather than guiding principle extraction. Deroy et al. [3] compared domain-speciﬁc mod-els and general LLMs across legal datasets. Steffes and Wiedemann [10] conceptualizedthe guiding principles generation task as a form of doctrinal summarization, reportinglimited effectiveness from prompt-based approaches and only moderate gains from ﬁne-tuned LLMs. Subsequent work [11] ﬁne-tuned LLMs on judgments enriched with le-gal entities and proposed a class-based evaluation framework. Despite these advances,generated principles still fall short of professional quality. Overall, prior studies sharekey gaps: they treat guiding principle generation as summarization, rely on surface-levelevaluation metrics, and face risks of hallucination [18] and doctrinal inaccuracy.
3. Model Selection and Fine-Tuning
We used GPT-4o as our primary advanced LLM, and LerLeoLM from Steffes et al. [11]
as the domain-speciﬁc baseline. It is a Mistral-based model ﬁne-tuned on 4,319 German
court decisions paired with guiding principles, enriched with legal entity information fol-lowing Leitner et al. [15], and represents the state of the art in German guiding principlegeneration. We used the publicly available outputs

4. Prompting Strategies
As baselines, we designed three simple prompts reﬂecting how non-expert users might
typically instruct an LLM:
•SimplePrompt-v1: “Y ou are a legal assistant. Write the guiding principle (headnote) for the following
court decision. ”
•SimplePrompt-v2: “Read the following German court decision and formulate a Leitsatz that reﬂects
the central legal principle. ”
•SimplePrompt-v3: “Y ou are a legal expert preparing a Leitsatz for a case law database. From the
court decision below, draft a Leitsatz (headnote) summarizing the key legal principle or doctrine de-
rived from the ruling. ”
To create the ExpertStructuredPrompt , we adapted the structured prompt design
proposed by Steffes et al. [10]. While it represents the most advanced legal expert-crafted
prompt available, it has two main limitations: (1) its question–answer format divergesfrom the concise, declarative style of expert-written guiding principles, and (2) it often

produces overly long or additional outputs. To overcome these issues, we introduced two
reﬁnements: UnlabeledStructuredPrompt , which removes the Q&A structure to align
more closely with expert drafting style, and UnlabeledStructuredPromptCoI , which re-
formulates the prompt into a chain-of-instructions (CoI) [5] format to enhance concise-ness and legal ﬁdelity.
The third prompting strategy, ChatCoI, is a structured prompt composed of a chain
of instructions (CoI), collaboratively created by a human and LLMs such as ChatGPTthrough interactive dialogue.
Interactive Dialogue for ChatCoI Prompt Creation
Human: What does “Leitsatz” mean in German court decisions?
LLM (ChatGPT -4o): [Explanation of the concept of a Leitsatz.]
Human: Y es, your understanding is correct. Now, could you suggest a chain-of-instructions (CoI)
prompt for an LLM to automatically generate a Leitsatz based on a given judgment?
LLM (ChatGPT -4o): [Proposed CoI instructions, e.g.:
T o generate a Leitsatz, you need to:
1.Understand the legal context – you must know what legal issue is being decided (e.g., remon-
stration, liability, ofﬁcial duties).
2.Identify the court’s conclusion – what did the court ultimately decide about that issue?
3.Extract the core legal principle – summarize that decision as a rule or principle in neutral legallanguage.]
Due to space limitations, we only reproduce the shortest version of ChatCoI (ChatCoI-
v1) in the paper, which is presented in the case box above. Using the same interactive
dialogue in separate new chats, we also generated two additional variants: ChatCoI-v2
and ChatCoI-v3. A few-shot variant, ChatCoI-3Examples , was also created, in which
the LLM was shown three example judgment–Leitsatz pairs, instructed to learn fromthem, and then asked to suggest a CoI prompt.
We additionally examined self-generated CoI, SelfCoI, in which the LLM au-
tonomously generated its own task-speciﬁc instructions during inference. In this setting,the LLM was ﬁrst prompted to design an internal “chain-of-instructions” for itself be-fore generating the ﬁnal Leitsatz. To account for variability, we executed the SelfCoI
procedure three times under identical conditions.

6. Experimental Results and Discussion
As shown in Figure1, ﬁne-tuned GPT -4o produced guiding principles whose lengths
most closely matched the “Gold” references. In contrast, both ExpertStructuredPrompt
and UnlabeledStructuredPrompt , which rely on expert-crafted structure, yielded sub-
stantially longer outputs, indicating that heavy structuring can encourage verbosity. Since
conciseness is a deﬁning feature of German Leits ¨atze, similarity in length can serve
as a partial indicator of stylistic adequacy, supporting the view that overly rigid expertprompting may undermine brevity and precision, thus addressing RQ2.
Table 1shows that ﬁne-tuned GPT -4o outperforms all other methods across lexi-
cal and semantic metrics. Among prompt-only approaches, ChatCoI-v2 performs best
overall. To address RQ3, Table 2compares automatic metrics with expert assessments.
The results indicate that traditional evaluation metrics are insufﬁcient for assessing theadequacy of generated guiding principles. Some outputs scored high on these metrics butwere judged unacceptable by human experts, while others with modest scores were con-sidered acceptable. LLM-based evaluation, using GPT -4o as a meta-evaluator, showed
stronger alignment with expert judgment, making it a more reliable method for legalquality assessment. Table 3presents results based on the Steffes et al. dataset to address
RQ1, examining whether advanced proprietary models can outperform domain-speciﬁcﬁne-tuned baselines. GPT -4o, even without any task-speciﬁc training, outperformed the
ﬁne-tuned LerLeoLM across all evaluation metrics. Notably, when GPT -4o was ﬁne-
tuned on just 100 examples (drawn from 2019 criminal and administrative cases), itachieved substantial performance gains despite the domain and temporal mismatch.
Overall, ﬁne-tuned GPT -4o delivers state-of-the-art performance. Among non-ﬁne-
tuned approaches, ChatCoI prompts stand out for their robustness. Even without expert
knowledge, users can co-create effective prompts through interactive prompting with anLLM. This highlights the practical potential of collaborative prompting in real-worldlegal NLP tasks. All prompts used in this study are available in the online repository.
7. Conclusion
In this paper, we present the ﬁrst systematic investigation of guiding principle genera-
tion using LLMs. Our results show that GPT-4o surpasses a domain-speciﬁc baselineeven with minimal and simple prompting, and that human–LLM collaborative promptcreation yields more doctrinally accurate outputs than expert-designed strategies. At thesame time, we highlight the limitations of surface-level metrics and propose LLM-basedevaluation as a scalable complement to expert review. While our study is limited bydataset size and jurisdiction, it establishes guiding principle generation as a distinct taskthat requires abstraction beyond summarization and opens new directions for researchon doctrinally faithful legal NLP .M.M. Abstract. This paper presents a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline
adapted to simulate the process of resolving legal cases. It introduces two novel ap-
proaches to enhance the RAG pipeline for legal reasoning: 1) problem generation,
which automatically creates ﬁctitious legal cases to improve retrieval performance,and 2) query rewriting, which reformulates user queries to better align with rele-
vant passages. These methods are evaluated on a legal reasoning dataset derivedfrom real U.S. civil procedure cases. Experiments conducted across different re-trieval methods (keyword search, tensor search, and hybrid search with re-ranking)and language models (GPT-4, SAULM, Llama-3 8B) highlight the beneﬁts of themore advanced RAG pipeline. Notably, the query rewriting approach consistentlyimproves performance by enhancing the alignment between queries and passages.
Keywords. Retrieval Augmented Generation, Legal Reasoning
1. Introduction
Artiﬁcial Intelligence has signiﬁcant potential to assist legal professionals by reducing
the time and effort required for complex legal tasks. Recent research has explored LLMs’capabilities in legal reasoning through prompting-based approaches for tasks such as le-gal judgment prediction [1], statutory reasoning [2], and legal exams [3], though lim-ited attention has been given to open-source models [4] or their integration with closed-source systems like GPT-4 [5]. RAG systems have evolved from basic retrieve-readpipelines [6] to advanced modular architectures with adaptive retrieval ﬂows [7–9],though these sophisticated approaches often require substantial computational resourcesand data [10, 11]. In the legal domain speciﬁcally, RAG-based systems have been devel-oped for statutory law inquiries in different languages [12, 13], highlighting the need formore comprehensive approaches to legal question-answering systems.
This paper addresses the task of legal reasoning over court cases, which involves
a two-step process: (1) retrieving the most pertinent passages from case text, such asstatutory provisions, precedents, or doctrinal explications, and (2) analyzing the retrievedmaterials to determine the most appropriate resolution. It introduces LR

2. Methodology
The proposed LR² pipeline builds upon the standard Retrieve-Read RAG architecture [6]
with two novel enhancements to address query-passage misalignment:Problem Generation: Instead of indexing original passages directly, the system auto-matically generates ﬁctitious legal cases from each original passage using an LLM. Foreach passage p
j, a corresponding ﬁctitious legal problem p′
jis generated. The retriever
then computes similarity scores s(q i,p′
j)between the user query and generated prob-
lems, ranking passages and returning the top-k original passages pjassociated with the
top-scores generated problems. This approach aims to better align the knowledge basecontent with typical user queries.Query Rewriting: An LLM reformulates the user input q
ito extract the most important
terms, producing a reﬁned query q′
i. The retrieval module then computes scores s(q′i,pj)
for each original passage, while the generation component uses the original user input qi
with the retrieved passages to produce the ﬁnal answer. This method enhances retrieval
effectiveness by improving query-passage alignment.
The dataset used for evaluation is derived from U.S. civil procedure domain [14, 15],
converted into a multiple-choice question answering format using Multiple-ChoicePrompting (MCP) [16]. Each instance consists of a legal problem question, context in-troduction, possible solution arguments, and annotated labels indicating correctness.
3. Results
GPT-4.1 demonstrated the best overall performance across all methods, with query
rewriting achieving the highest scores (Accuracy: 0.632, Precision: 0.620, Recall: 0.611,F1: 0.613). For GPT-4, query rewriting yielded substantial improvements (Accuracy:0.590, F1: 0.550) compared to the baseline Retrieve-Read approach (Accuracy: 0.515,F1: 0.414). Llama-3 8B showed modest improvements with query rewriting (Accuracy:0.410, F1: 0.402) over baseline (Accuracy: 0.401, F1: 0.382). SAULM, despite beingpre-trained on legal domain, demonstrated lower generalization capability in zero-shotreasoning tasks. The hybrid BM25 with tensor re-ranking consistently outperformedother methods. Query rewriting with this hybrid approach achieved the best retrievalmetrics (MRR: 0.368, R@1: 0.234, R@5: 0.563, R@10: 0.688), outperforming the base-line Retrieve-Read method (MRR: 0.337, R@1: 0.219, R@10: 0.633). Problem genera-tion yielded modest improvements (MRR: 0.359, R@1: 0.211) but did not match queryrewriting’s effectiveness. Methods relying solely on dense vector representations consis-tently underperformed compared to keyword-based and hybrid approaches, suggestingthat explicit keyword matching remains crucial for legal information retrieval.

Abstract. Argument Mining (AM) [1], the task of extracting arguments and their
relations (e.g. attacks, supports) from text, has lead to potential applications of
formal models of argumentation on real-world scenarios. However, AM methods
largely depend on Machine Learning (ML) techniques, which require high-qualityannotated data. This poses a signiﬁcant limitation in domains like legal reason-ing, where annotated corpora are extremely scarce. Current legal AM research re-lies almost entirely on a single dataset from the European Court of Human Rights(ECHR) [2], limiting the development of robust, argumentation-driven automatedlegal reasoning systems. Addressing this data scarcity is essential for advancingcomputational legal argumentation. To address this challenge, this paper brieﬂy de-scribes some preliminary results that demonstrate the promising potential of LLMsto assist legal experts in annotating additional legal corpora. This advancementpaves the way for more robust, argumentation-driven automated reasoning systemsin the legal domain. More details on our approach and experimental results are pro-vided in [3].
Keywords. Legal argumentation, Argument mining, LLMs
1. Argumentation Pipeline
Using 9 short and 6 long texts from the ECHR dataset as a baseline, we have queried an
LLM (meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct [4]) to extract arguments from these texts,
aiming to identify how many original (annotated) arguments are generated by the model.Since LLMs may rephrase the content, we measured the similarity between originaland generated arguments using the sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 similarity
model. A generated argument is considered a match if its similarity to an original oneexceeds a threshold τ. We tested different pipeline variants (outlined in Figure 1), with
or without providing examples of arguments.

2. Experiments
Our initial experiments show that the ﬁrst pipeline (direct extraction of arguments from
legal texts using examples) is the most effective. The number of arguments generatedby the LLM and their mean and maximal number of premises are the most similar tothose in the annotated dataset. So, we focus on this pipeline to evaluate similarity andmatching ratios between original and LLM-generated arguments. After a ﬁrst set of ex-periments, we introduced an improved prompt, which yields better results on two textsamples (short and long texts). Although matched arguments generally show high sim-ilarity (over 80% on average), many generated arguments do not appear in the originaldataset. Our improved prompt allows to reduce this phenomenon. 3. Conclusion
The evaluation of our system shows promising capabilities for LLMs to help identify-
ing arguments in legal text, which would greatly reduce the burden of annotation. Be-sides the results presented in this extended abstract, we have also evaluated anotherLLM (Equall/Saul-7B-Instruct-v1 [5]) and a state-of-the-art AM approach (ArgueMap-
per/ArgueBuf [6,7]), as well as the similarity between claims and premises of the ex-tracted arguments. As part of our future work, we plan to evaluate the efﬁciency of ourproposed pipeline as a support tool for legal experts in the annotation of legal texts. Ad-ditionally, we aim to assess its versatility by extending its application beyond the ECHRdataset, with the goal of generalizing the approach to a broader range of legal domains.C. Abstract. This study introduces Pro-Judice, a benchmark to assess how large lan-
guage models align with procedural fairness in judicial contexts. Using criminal
case data from China and US legal traditions, it reveals that models’ proceduralfairness perceptions vary by legal context of test dataset, model architecture andversion differences, and dataset-model interaction.
Keywords. Large Language Models (LLMs), Procedural Fairness, Judicial Alignment,
Legal Tradition
1. Introduction
In legal AI, judgment prediction is a key focus, but concerns remain due to the
black-box nature of large language models. [1][2][3][4][5]. While prior work empha-sizes human-computer decision making and distributive justice, procedural fairness isunderexplored.[6][7][8][9][10][11] [12] [13][14]Procedures are vital for legitimacy andrights protection, especially in criminal law. Legal traditions differ: civil law stressesfact-ﬁnding, common law values adversarial fairness.[15] AI models may inherit suchbiases from training data.[16][17][18]This study introduces the Pro-Judice benchmark,
grounded in Rawls’ theory[19] and international human rights standards, using criminallaw data from China and the U.S. It evaluates LLMs’ alignment with nine proceduralfairness principles, evaluating ﬁve models—DeepSeek V3, DeepSeek R1, and Qwen-2.5 from China, and GPT-4o and Llama-3.3 from the U.S. Results show that fairnessperceptions vary by legal tradition of model and dataset, and dataset-model interaction.

Towards Interpretable Hierarchical Graph
Neural Networks in Criminal Law
Thiago DAL PONTa,c,1
,Isabela SABOb
,Maite VIEIRAb
,Jomi H ¨UBNERa

and Aires ROVERb
aAutomation and Systems Department, Federal University of Santa Catarina, Brazil
bDepartment of Law, Federal University of Santa Catarina, Brazil
cAlmaAI Research Centre, University of Bologna, Italy
Abstract. This paper proposes and evaluates a method for interpreting hierarchical
graph neural network (GNN) nodes created from criminal law texts. We optimise
a hierarchical GNN with extra loss functions to generate coherent abstract nodesfrom Brazilian habeas corpus data. Four concept grounding (CG) methods (utilis-ing semantic similarity and large language models (LLMs)) are evaluated for giv-ing names to these nodes. Quantitative results demonstrate that optimisation im-proves the quality of abstractions and predictive performance. Qualitative expertevaluation favoured labels based on LLMs. This dual approach (optimisation andgrounding) provides a framework towards more trustworthy and explainable legalAI systems.
Keywords. Criminal Law, Interpretability, Textual Graphs, Concept Grounding
1. Introduction
Explainability is crucial in high-stakes domains, such as law, where transparency is re-
quired for due process [1,2]. However, standard natural language processing (NLP) meth-ods for explainable artiﬁcial intelligence (XAI), such as SHAP [3] or LIME [4], oftenprovide feature attributions as lists of important but structurally unrelated words. Thisfails to capture the relational nature of legal writing [5].
Relational explanations using graph neural networks (GNNs) on text graphs (where
nodes are words and edges are dependencies) offer a promising alternative by explic-itly modelling text structure [6]. However, while hierarchical GNNs can learn high-levelabstractions by grouping nodes, the conceptual meaning of these abstractions is oftenunclear, necessitating concept grounding (CG), i.e. mapping these abstractions to real-world concepts. Our work uniquely combines GNN training optimisation aiming at co-herent abstractions with a comparative evaluation of CG strategies, building on recentwork in legal AI transparency [7,8] and GNN interpretability [9,10]. We thus investi-gate: to what extent can we map the abstract nodes of a hierarchical GNN into natural
language to explain how it reaches its predictions in criminal law cases?

Our methodology involves generating and interpreting hierarchical representations
from a corpus of Brazilian Supreme Court pre-trial detention decisions, framed as a bi-

1503 not released (see [11]). Decisions become graph structures using dependency pars-ing [12], where nodes are words (initialised with pre-trained legal GloVe embeddings,see [13,14]) and edges are syntactic dependencies. We employed DiffPool [15], a hierar-chical GNN, to learn multi-level graph representations by clustering words (level 0) intoabstract nodes at higher levels (Figure 1; abstract nodes to be grounded: A, B and C).

The optimisation metric was theInterpretability-Aware Performance Score (IAPS), ahybrid metric balancing Macro F1-score with abstrac-tion quality). We then propose four Concept Ground-ing (CG) methods: (1) semantic similarity to the aver-age embedding of assigned words; (2) semantic simi-larity to the abstract node’s embedding; (3) LLM-based (LLaMa 3.3 70B); and (4) usingthe top assigned word.
Quantitatively, Macro F1 was measured against baselines, and IAPS assesses ab-
stract node quality using Concept Completeness (expressiveness) and Concept Confor-mity (purity) [9]. For qualitative assessment, two legal experts evaluated 18 abstractnodes on semantic coherence (1-5 Likert scale) and ranked the labels from all four CGmethods based on faithfulness, speciﬁcity, and plausibility.
2. Results, Discussion and Conclusion
Our optimised Diffpool (Macro-F1 0.821) outperformed standard GCN (0.817) base-
lines, while improving abstract node quality (Concept Conformity rose to 0.890, p<
0.05; Concept Completeness was 1.000).
Qualitatively, experts rated the GNN’s abstractions as only moderately coherent
(2.82/5). But, they clearly preferred CG labels from the LLM-Based and Similarity fromAssigned Nodes methods, while the poor performance of using the GNN’s own abstractembeddings directly for similarity search indicates they lack direct semantic grounding.
Returning to our research question, abstract nodes of a hierarchical GNN may be
translated into natural language to a moderate but promising extent. Our dual approachis a viable path towards more transparent legal AI, with LLM-based and semantic searchmethods showing the most success. The moderate coherence of the learned abstractionsand the small scale of our expert evaluation are key limitations requiring further valida-tion. Future work will focus on integrating subgraph explanations (e.g., SubgraphX [18]),multi-level explanations [19], regression [20] and expanding expert evaluation.

Abstract. We have developed a system, based on prioritized default logic, for repre-
senting legal rules and their exceptions. Our system can help the law practitioner’s
reasoning in presence of scenarios that induce an exception to a rule. When thereis no known exception to the rule r
1for a scenario, the system can help the user to
adapt the exception r′
2to a general rule r2.
Keywords. Default Logic, Handling exceptions, System description
Legal reasoning is highly sensitive to exceptions, i.e.situations where a general rule
would imply a given decision, but a more speciﬁc context leads to a different decision.

Abstract. This work introduces the formal framework DLRisk, based on Defeasible
Deontic Logic, for assessing how fundamental rights are balanced under the EU AI
Act when new systems are developed. This approach enables qualitative, scenario-
aware reasoning by ordering rights, capturing demotions triggered by factual condi-
tions, and detecting collisions between rights and deployment contexts. The result is
an explainable assessment of trade-offs that supports compliance analysis and risk
mitigation.
Keywords. Risk assessment, Defeasible deontic logic, Fundamental rights
1. Introduction
Risk assessment is the core idea behind the European AI Act (AIA), the normative
framework that has been designed to regulate the introduction of AI systems on the basis
of their risk proﬁles. However, a key methodological issue remains: how can we evaluate
and mitigate the impact of technical hazards on fundamental rights?
This question belongs to a long tradition on balancing conﬂicting interests, where
technical progress may represent an issue for rights’ protection. In the context of the AI
Act risk mitigation, this work tries to propose a methodology to investigate how speciﬁc
features of an AI system may demote certain rights or generate collision between them.
This project aims to be a balancing test through which legal experts can evaluate whether
the beneﬁts of an AI introduction overweighs or not detriments.
Following [ 1,2] we argue for an analysis based on risk scenarios involving interactions
among multiple risk factors, rather than a scope-oriented characterization. Building on
[3], we thus propose a way to formalize a balancing evaluation with formal method, to
avoid using opaque approaches to perform an interpretable analysis, that must support a
human-in-the-loop approach.

telligence (AI) systems are safe and trustworthy has led to a fragmented landscape
of AI governance. The European Union (EU) is a key actor in the development ofsuch policies and guidelines. The rapid advancement of Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) technologies, coupled with an in-
creasing number of AI-related incidents, has positioned AI as a key topic in global pol-icymaking discourse. The European Union (EU) has become a leader in this landscape,particularly after the enactment of its AI regulation, the EU AI Act [1], in 2024. However,

multiple documents were issued both before and after the adoption of the AI Act that

These range from the EU-High Level Expert Group(HLEG)’s “Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI” (2019) [2], to the guidelines issued bythe European Commission in 2025 on prohibited AI practices (C(2025) 5052 ﬁnal) [3].While EU AI policies are expected to be aligned in pursuit of a common vision of trust-worthy AI, they adopt distinct approaches towards AI governance, which is manifestedin their focus area (e.g. AI innovation, risk management, sector-speciﬁc requirements),their degree of normativity (binding, non-binding), enforcement mechanisms, and tech-nical and organisational measures they prescribe. There is also a temporal dimension toconsider, since these policies were developed at different times and therefore may notaddress recent advances in AI capabilities.
In this paper, we aim to uncover AI governance concepts within the EU AI policy
landscape through identiﬁcation of recurring topics and themes, both shared and diver-gent. The research question this paper explores is: What are the prevalent themes in the
EU AI policies and guidelines post-2018 concerning AI governance?
One way of addressing the research question is through the use of qualitative the-
matic analysis approaches [4] from social sciences. Since thematic analysis is conducted
manually by domain experts, it can yield nuanced and high-quality insights, however itis inherently subjective, time-intensive, and difﬁcult to scale. To mitigate these limita-tions, we adopt unsupervised topic modelling techniques from natural language process-
ing (NLP), which enable identiﬁcation of frequent topics in large text corpora, in combi-nation with thematic analysis to interpret, validate, and provide context to the discoveredtopics.
In the remainder of this paper, we ﬁrst review the body of work on the analysis of AI
policies in section 2. Then, in section 3 we discuss our methodology that combines topicmodelling and thematic analysis approaches. section 4 provides the identiﬁed AI topicsand themes. Finally, section 5 concludes the paper by discussing our plan for future work.
2. Related Work
There is a body of work that analyses the content of AI policies and guidelines to deter-
mine the degree of consensus (or divergence) as well as the gaps in AI governance andethical AI principles within the growing body of AI policies. These studies apply quali-tative thematic analysis, quantitative content analysis (often using topic modelling algo-rithms such as LDA and BERT), or a combination of both. In the following, we reviewsome of the related work on AI policies that utilised these approaches.
2.1. Automated Analysis of AI Policies via Topic ModellingA pioneering work [5] within the realm of NLP-based AI policies’ analysis uses topical
distributions from LDA to perform clustering over 12 national AI strategies, and use thecluster information to determine the strategic priorities of various governments in the AIrace. It is important to note that this analysis was performed over some of the earliestavailable documents covering strategic directions laid by national governments with re-spect to AI; and hence there is also more coverage on leadership in AI deployment forinnovation. 2.2. Combination of Automated and Manual Analysis of AI policiesRoche et al. [8] used a combination of automated data analytics tools and manual con-

Schiff et al.[9] analysed the degree of global consensus on ethical AI principles by manual codingof AI documents published by public sector, private organisations, and NGOs, followedby a quantitative analysis of the coding. On a superﬁcial level, this may seemsimilar to the analysis by Kajava et al. [12]. This presents a complex andchanging body of texts that must be monitored and analysed to understand changes tothe expectations and effect of the original Act. 3. Methodology
As shown in Figure 1, our methodology comprises four key steps: (1) corpus creation
of EU AI policy documents, (2) manual thematic analysis, (3) unsupervised topic mod-elling and (4) interdisciplinary expert analysis of topics to identify themes and deriveadditional insights. For the purpose of this paper, we consider a topic as a concept iden-
tiﬁed automatically by a topic modeller from text (algorithm-driven), and a theme as a
broad interpretable semantic concept derived through expert interpretation, either fromthe topics generated by a topic modeller or directly from the text itself (human-driven).

Abstract. In the devolved legal system of the United Kingdom (UK), legislative
provisions may apply differently across regions such as England, Wales, Scotland,
and Northern Ireland. Accurately determining this territorial scope is essential forlegal interpretation and AI-assisted legal tools. However, metadata capturing juris-dictional applicability is inconsistently format, as only a few Acts include Terri-torial Application Annexes. This study presents a case study using the EducationAct 2005 to evaluate the accuracy of automated methods for identifying territorialscope. We found that only 46.9% of sections matched in jurisdictional coverage.The best-performing approach achieved nearly 80% accuracy, showing that LLMscan effectively support scalable and explainable territorial disambiguation.
Keywords. Territorial Disambiguation, Legal—DocML, Large Language Models
1. Introduction
Legislation in the UK operates under a devolved structure, dividing authority between
England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. Determining where a provision ap-plies—its territorial scope—is vital for legal interpretation and compliance automation.The National Archives provides statutes in Akoma Ntoso XML (LegalDocML) format,
using ¡extent¿ tags to indicate territorial coverage. However, practical application maybe narrower: a section marked as extending to England and Wales (E+W) may, in ef-fect, apply only to England, depending on institutional references or legal context. Thisleads to ambiguity when <extent> alone is used for territorial inference. The Education
Act 2005, which includes a detailed Territorial Application Annex, provides a uniqueground truth to evaluate and improve automated territorial scope extraction using AI-based methods. As highlighted in the paper, many Acts lack such annexes, making ter-ritorial classiﬁcation a manual and non-scalable task. This motivated the exploration of

2. Methodology
This study used the Education Act 2005 as a benchmark to evaluate automated ap-
proaches for territorial classiﬁcation. Each section of the Act was extracted from itsLegalDocML representation and paired with its corresponding ground-truth jurisdic-tion(s) from the Territorial Application Annex. The dataset was structured to include sec-tion text, hierarchical context (Part/Chapter titles), and ¡extent¿ metadata. Four progres-sively enriched methods were evaluated: (1) Extent-tag baseline, which directly mapped¡extent¿ territories to predicted scope; (2) Named Entity Recognition (NER), which usedjurisdictional mentions to reﬁne classiﬁcation; (3) LLM-based inference, where largelanguage models (DeepSeek-R1 8B and 32B) were prompted using structured contextto infer territorial scope; and (4) LLM with legal knowledge cues, which augmentedprompts with domain-speciﬁc rules (e.g., references to ¨Secretary of State ¨ımply England,
¨Estyn ¨suggests Wales). Model outputs were compared against the Annex, and accuracy
was computed across all 128 sections to assess performance improvements across meth-ods. All code and evaluation tools are publicly available
2.
3. Results and Discussion
The baseline extent tag approach achieved 46.9% accuracy, revealing that current meta-
data does not reliably represent territorial scope. NER improved performance to 61.7%,while the LLM-based methods achieved 63–73% accuracy. When enriched with legalknowledge, accuracy reached nearly 80%. These results demonstrate that combiningstructured context and simple legal cues can signiﬁcantly improve AI-based territorialinference. However, manually embedding knowledge in prompts is not scalable, empha-sizing the need for integrating legal knowledge graphs [2] in future research.
4. Conclusion and Future Work
Manual identiﬁcation of territorial applicability in UK legislation is slow and challenging
due to nuanced legal language and cross-references. This study shows that AI modelscan analyse statutory text to suggest likely territorial scope, reducing dependence onmanually crafted annexes. Future work will focus on exploring more techniques to addexternal knowledge [3] and enhancing interpretability so that each AI-generated decisionis supported with clear reasoning and can be easily veriﬁed.

Extracting Unwritten Sentencing Rules
from Czech Higher Courts’ Verdicts
Tom´aˇsK N A Pa,1
aFaculty of Law, Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic
Abstract. Czech courts operate without formal sentencing guidelines, relying on
implicit principles that remain unmapped and inconsistently applied. This poster
presents an early-stage project developing a four-phase pipeline to extract unwrittensentencing rules from Czech higher court decisions. The methodology combines:(i) thematic analysis for reasoning pattern identiﬁcation, (ii) LLM-Based rule ex-traction and classiﬁcation of rules (iii) cross-decision semantic matching and cita-tion network analysis, and (iv) planned expert validation with criminal law schol-ars. The pipeline aims to reveal how principles emerge and propagate across thecourt hierarchy, from district courts to the Supreme Court. This work will providethe ﬁrst systematic mapping of Czech implicit sentencing rules and a transferablemethodology for other criminal law jurisdictions.
Keywords. Sentencing principles, higher courts, judicial discretion, legal argument
mining, semantic role labeling, citation network analysis
1. Introduction and Motivation
Unlike continental jurisdictions with formal sentencing guidelines (e.g., Finland [1]),
Czech higher courts lack explicit frameworks for principle-setting. While appeals areﬁled in approximately 10% of criminal cases, with courts modifying 25% of appealeddecisions (primarily sentences), the Supreme Court generally does not review sentenc-ing, leaving appellate courts as the de facto source of sentencing jurisprudence [2]. Yetresearch on post-communist Europe has focused on statutory frameworks rather than onhow these courts actually create and apply rules, making systematic analysis essential tounderstand actual sentencing [3,2]. This project uses LLM-enhanced analysis to extractimplicit sentencing principles from the decisions of Czech appellate courts, high courts,the Supreme Court, and the Constitutional Court, providing the ﬁrst computational map-ping of how principles are articulated and propagated across the court hierarchy.
2. Methods
As visualized in Figure 1, research is based on a four-phase interpretable pipeline that
processes criminal sentencing decisions from Czech higher courts (Appellate Courts,High Courts, Supreme Court, and Constitutional Court) to identify and validate unwrittenrules while maintaining transparency for legal experts:

Phase I: Thematic Analysis. The decision corpus is thematically analyzed to identify
recurring reasoning patterns and normative themes. Structured prompting helps distin-
guish general principles from case-speciﬁc facts and outline initial candidate rules [4].
Phase II: LLM-Based Rule Extraction and Classiﬁcation. Instruction-tuned large
language models transform identiﬁed themes into candidate IF–THEN rules. Through
iterative prompt engineering, few-shot examples from domain-speciﬁc terminology (ag-gravating/mitigating circumstances, proportionality principle) enable the models to clas-sify outputs as genuine principles or case-speciﬁc holdings [5].
Phase III: Cross-Decision Analysis. Validated rules are traced across decisions via se-
mantic similarity (sentence-BERT for Czech legal texts), citation-network analysis cap-
turing “following” and “distinguishing” relations, and temporal tracking of doctrinal evo-lution [6,7].
Phase IV: Expert Evaluation and Reﬁnement. Criminal-law experts assess doctrinal
accuracy, applicability, and consistency with the Criminal Code. Their feedback informs
the iterative reﬁnement and ﬁnal synthesis of ﬁndings.

Jia LIUa,b,1 and Jianhao TANG  a,b 
a

Abstract.  This study introduces LeAK-GraphRAG, a framework that leverages 
knowledge graphs tailored for legal papers to enhance the semantic understanding 
of large language models (LLMs) regarding specialized legal academic knowledge and reduce hallucinations. Using a corpus of legal papers, we automatically 
extracted entities and relations with LLMs to construct a knowledge graph and 
systematically evaluated the performance of three retrieval methods and five LLMs. 
Experimental results demonstrated that the hybrid retrieval strategy achieved the 
best overall performance across most evaluation metrics, effectively combining 
semantic similarity with the structural relations of knowledge graph entities. 
Keywords.  GraphRAG, hybrid retrieval, legal information retrieval, knowledge 
graph, hallucinations 
1. Introduction 
In specialized areas of legal research, the kn owledge provided by large language models 
(LLMs) remains fragmented, lacking domai n-specific expertise.  Therefore, LLMs 
frequently hallucinate when addressing specialized legal academic questions, often 
producing inaccurate, irrelevant, or fabricated information [ 1]. Retrieval-augmented 
generation (RAG) combines LLMs with ex ternal knowledge bases, improving the 
accuracy and relevance of generated content. Its effectiveness has al so been validated in 
the legal domain [ 2,3,4]. On this basis, graph retrieval-augmented generation 
(GraphRAG)  [ 5,6] integrates the relational reasoning capability of knowledge graphs 
with the semantic understanding capability of  vector retrieval, further mitigating the 
hallucination issue in LLMs [ 7]. Considering that construc ting knowledge graphs from 
domain-specific legal papers c ould enhance the output capabilities of LLMs in academic 
legal contexts, this study proposes a GraphRAG framework—LeAK-GraphRAG2.

2. Methods and Results 
In the knowledge graph cons truction stage, we used th e China National Knowledge 
Infrastructure as our data source and applied the followi ng search formula: topic = 
(“training data” OR “dataset” OR “artific ial intelligence training data”) AND (“legal 
regulation” OR “regulatory framework” OR “governance” OR  “law” OR “risk”). This 
search retrieved 29 relevant papers, which were divided into text chunks for entity 
relation extraction, as shown in Figure 1. Th e resulting knowledge graph comprised 1163 
entities and 1113 relations. Additionally, 1 091 legal question-answer pairs were 
generated based on the extr acted text chunks, serving as test datasets to support 
evaluation. Evaluation metrics included dive rsity, comprehensiveness, empowerment, 
directness, semantic similarity, and accuracy . The semantic similarity was computed and 
evaluated using BERT, while we used DeepSeek  to determine the accuracy of the 
answers and invited legal experts to manually compare and verify the accuracy rate of 
each model using different retrieval methods. In the knowledge retrieval stage, we 
adopted three retrieval methods. Vector r etrieval achieves seman tic matching retrieval 
by calculating the cosine similar ity between query text and the textual descriptions of 
entities and relationships in the knowledge graph. Cypher retrieval integ rates semantic 
matching with graph structural features, calculating a hybrid score using vector similarity 
and graph relationship weights. Hybrid retr ieval merges results from both methods. In 
the answer generation stage, we employed selected LLMs to generate answers for legal questions in the test dataset, comb ined with relevant texts obtained in the previous stage. 
Experimental results indicated that hybrid retrieval achieved the highest scores for 
comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and directness across the LLMs because 
hybrid retrieval combined the f lexibility of textual semantics with the structure of graph 
relationships, compensating for the inadequacy of vector retrieval in handling structured 
relational information and overcoming the limitations of C ypher retrieval in capturing 
unstructured information. The semantic simi larity scores and accuracy rates among the 
five LLMs were generally high, indicating th at the answers generated by all models were 
closely aligned with the corresponding reference answers.

3. Conclusion 
This study proposed LeAK-GraphRAG, a GraphRAG framework  on legal academic 
knowledge. Evaluation results demonstrated that LeAK-GraphRAG could enhance the 
output quality of LLMs in the legal acad emic domain and reduce hallucinations.

A GraphRAG Approach to Enhancing the 
Ability of Causal Reasoning in 
Autonomous Driving Cases 
Jia LIUa,b,1 and Xingtong CHEN  a 
a
 Law School, Huazhong Univers ity of Science and Technology, Wuhan, Hubei, China 
b
 Hubei Judicial Big Da ta Research Center, Wuhan, Hubei, China 
Abstract.  Large language models (LLMs) are significantly limited in causal 
reasoning in the legal domain. Determining legal liability in autonomous-driving 
traffic accidents inherently involves complex causal relationships, thereby providing 
a typical scenario for exploring and enhancing the causal reasoning capabilities of LLMs in legal contexts. In this study, GraphRAG is employed to provide more 
accurate and interpretable causal reasoning pathways for LLMs to determine legal 
liability, thereby enhancing their causal reasoning capabilities in the context of 
determining autonomous-driving traffic accident liability. We construct a 
knowledge graph from expert-annotated judicial documents using Neo4j and 
integrate it with LLMs using the LangChain framework. After referencing the legal causal reasoning paths retrieved from similar cases, LLMs could generate causal 
reasoning processes and final legal liability determinations for unresolved cases. 
This study could provide insights into judicial practices in autonomous-driving traffic accidents and advance the application of LLM-based causal reasoning in the 
legal domain. 
Keywords.  GraphRAG, causal reasoning, knowledge graph, autonomous driving, 
legal Q&A 
1. Introduction 
Large language models (LLMs) exhibit high  hallucinations and poor interpretability in 
legal question-answering tasks [ 1]. These shortcomings are particularly pronounced in 
tasks that require legal causal reasoning [ 2]. Determining legal liability in autonomous-
driving traffic accidents involv es complex causal relationships [ 3], providing a typical 
scenario for investigating the causal reasoni ng capabilities of LLMs in the legal domain. 
Accordingly, this study aims to  utilize GraphRAG to provide LLMs with more accurate 
and interpretable causal reasoning pathway s for answering legal liability determination 
questions, thereby enhancing their caus al reasoning capabilities in determining 
autonomous-driving traffic accident liability[ 4,5,6 ].

2. Methods 
We use publicly available judicial documents on autonomous-driving traffic accidents 
from China Judgments Online as the foundational corpus. These documents contain 
comprehensive information, including case  facts, adjudication bases, adjudication 
reasoning, and adjudication results. Using tech niques such as knowledge extraction and 
fusion, we construct a knowledge graph us ing Neo4j. To obtain more accurate and 
comprehensive information that better aligns with legal logic [ 7,8], we integrate relevant 
laws and regulations [ 9] applicable to autonomous-driving cases and rely on legal experts 
to annotate legal causal reasoning  paths for cases in the knowledge graph. Annotations 
include legal causal types (e.g., direct and indirect causation) and legal causal 
relationship patterns (e.g., sing le cause-single effect and mu ltiple cause-multiple effects). 
We construct a test dataset c ontaining information on auto nomous-driving cases and 
questions regarding legal liability determination, organizing legal experts to answer these 
questions. The cases in the test set cover complex scen arios involving multiple parties, 
behaviors, and causal relatio nships potentially influenced by factors such as vehicle 
malfunctions and human intervention errors . Based on LangChain, LLMs are integrated 
with the knowledge graph. LLMs retrieve relev ant information (e.g., legal causal 
reasoning paths) from cases similar to th e unresolved case in the knowledge graph [ 10]. 
By referencing legal causal reasoning path s from similar cases, LLMs generate these 
paths for unresolved cases and answer questions  related to legal liability determination 
[11]. The overall process is illustrated in Figure 1. To further enhance LLM 
interpretability, our improved approach offe rs users traceable similar case-matching 
analysis processes, causal reasoning paths that  adhere to legal logic, and reliable liability 
determination results when an swering questions. The results obtained by the proposed 
approach will be evaluated against thos e generated by only LLMs, both quantitatively 
and qualitatively, using the answers provided by legal experts as reference answers. Specifically, the causal reasoning capabilities of  the proposed appr oach will be assessed 
from aspects such as comprehensiven ess, interpretability, and accuracy.

3. Conclusion 
In this study, GraphRAG is applied to enhance the accura cy and interpretability of LLMs 
for legal causal reasoning tasks in a specific leg al scenario. This approach could offer 
insights into judicial practices in autonomous-driving traf fic accidents and advance the 
application of LLM-based causal re asoning in the legal domain.

Automated Identiﬁcation of Criminal
Offences from Case Descriptions Using
Ontologies, Rules and LLMs
Jelena MA TKOVI ´Ca, Marko MARKOVI ´Caand Stevan GOSTOJI ´Ca
aUniversity of Novi Sad, Faculty of T echnical Sciences, Serbia
Abstract. This paper presents a system that automatically identiﬁes criminal of-
fences from Montenegrin court decisions. Factual attributes are extracted using
LLMs and mapped to an OWL ontology with SWRL rules to infer applicable le-gal provisions and sanctions. Evaluation conducted on a dataset of court decisionsdemonstrates consistently high levels of accuracy and recall, conﬁrming the feasi-bility of integrating LLM-based factual extraction with ontology-driven legal rea-soning.
Keywords. rule-based reasoning, prompt engineering, automated legal reasoning,
criminal law, legal ontology
1. Introduction
Automatically identifying criminal offences from unstructured legal narratives is chal-
lenging due to complex language and variability in narrative expression of factual de-scriptions. Previous work has demonstrated that ontology-based reasoning can supportautomated decision-making in the criminal domain [1,2]. In this study, we integrate largelanguage model extraction with an OWL ontology [3] and SWRL rules [4] to identifytheft-related offences (Articles 239–242 of the Criminal Code of Montenegro [5]) fromMontenegrin court decisions. ChatGPT [6] is used to extract factual attributes, which are
instantiated within the ontology.
2. Methodology
Our dataset consists of 2,357 basic court decisions from the ofﬁcial judiciary portal [7],
of which 841 contained at least one theft-related offence. The system represents legalknowledge using a three-layer ontology comprising the Legal Norm Layer, which en-codes articles and their hierarchical structure; the Legal Case Layer, which captures en-tities such as offenders, victims, and offence elements (e.g., intent, execution, and cir-cumstances); and the SWRL Layer, containing 42 rules that infer applicable legal pro-visions based on instantiated facts. The ontology and rules are available online [8]. Fac-tual attributes are extracted from unstructured case descriptions using 28 prompt ques-tions posed to ChatGPT. 4. Discussion and Conclusion
Combining LLM-based extraction with ontology and SWRL reasoning achieves high
recall and reliable classiﬁcation of theft-related offences. Most errors arise from semanticambiguity and overgeneralised LLM outputs. The system demonstrates feasibility as adecision-support tool for preliminary legal qualiﬁcation. Future work will expand theontology to additional offences and explore local LLM deployment to preserve sensitivedata.

Principles of Law: LLMs vs RegEx
Marianna MOLINARIa,b,c,1, Ilaria Angela AMANTEAb,
Marinella QUARANTAa,b,cand Guido GOVERNATORId
aUniversity of Bologna - LaST-JD, Legal Studies Dept.

dCentral Queensland University
Abstract. Principles of law (PoLs) oﬀer a framework for case interpretation and
ensure legal consistency, especially in areas lacking speciﬁc legislation. Courts use
PoLs to establish binding precedents that guide decision-making. However, PoLsare expressed in a non-standard way in rulings, making them diﬃcult to iden-tify at a glance without interpretative reading. Our study tested ChatGPT, Claude,and DeepSeek in extracting PoLs, verifying their results with Regular Expressions(RegEx). While Large Language Models (LLMs) showed promise, their outputsrequired signiﬁcant expert oversight, revealing limitations in legal research, partic-ularly in terms of accuracy and quantity.
Keywords. Principles of Law, LLMs, RegEx, Extraction.
1. Introduction and Methodology
When judges encounter new demands not addressed by existing laws, they create PoLs
through their decisions [1,2]. Once stated or reaﬃrmed in a judgment, PoLs becomeprecedents [3]. Precedents promote legal certainty and fairness, particularly when lawsare absent or unclear [4,5]. Analyzing precedents to identify the core PoL(s) is crucial,as judgments are typically written in various styles that aﬀect how PoLs and relatedcitations are presented, making prompt identiﬁcation challenging [6]. After addressing theissue [7,8], we focused on automatically extracting PoLs using ChatGPT [9], comparingits performance with RegEx [10,11]. This paper extends the comparative analysis byincluding various LLMs and conducts a retrospective evaluation with a RegEx baseline,generated by ChatGPT and applied via a simple text editor. This approach guaranteesthat the process can be reproduced and veriﬁed for falsiﬁability [12,13]. As tested, weprompted ChatGPT to generate a Python script [14] using RegEx to extract paragraphswith quoted text and speciﬁc keywords [15].The script processed .docx ﬁles, extractedPoLs, and outputted a separate CSV ﬁle for each document. PoLs were extracted from29 randomly selected Italian judgments in .docx format from the De Jure database.The judgments were divided into two sets: originals, annotated manually by three legalexperts, and copies, processed using LLMs and RegEx. Annotation followed guidelinesidentifying: explicit direct PoLs, clearly stated in quotation marks, often starting with anintroductory phrase, and explicitly connected to a prior citation; explicit indirect PoLs,

3. ConclusionsThis study highlights that while LLMs can provide a general overview of judgments, they
remain susceptible to bias, hallucinations, and inaccuracies. These issues are especiallyproblematic when dealing with PoLs, which can be mixed, reported partially, or confusedwith passages that are technically correct but do not constitute actual PoLs (Not-PoLs).Since the validity of PoLs depends on accuracy, it is crucial for domain experts to remaininvolved in overseeing their extraction.

Packaging Thematic Analysis as an AI
Workﬂow for Legal Research
V ojtˇech POURa,1,2
aFaculty of Law, Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic
Abstract. This work-in-progress paper introduces a reusable system that opera-
tionalises thematic analysis for legal research as a reproducible, agentic workﬂow.
Researchers upload a JSON corpus keyed by case identiﬁers; plain-language intent
(scope, granularity, focus, presentation) is mapped to a ﬁxed sequence of phases or-
chestrated from the frontend. A lightweight web UI streams intermediate outputs and
offers optional checkpoints with reversible edits. The workﬂow is model-agnostic,
multilingual, and stabilises codebooks and candidate themes without ad-hoc prompt
retuning on representative case-law datasets. Concretely, I package and expose in a
frontend the approach explored by Drápal, Westermann, and Šavelka and collabora-
tors. The current prototype is fully operational through candidate theme generation
(Phase 3); the ﬁnal consolidation and assignment stages (Phases 3b–4) are planned
for completion by JURIX. Overall, the system lowers time-to-ﬁrst-theme, improves
reﬁnement safety, and increases portability across jurisdictions and languages.
Keywords. Thematic analysis, legal research, LLMs, qualitative coding, agentic
workﬂows, case law, NLP
1. Introduction and Motivation
Thematic analysis (TA) identiﬁes and interprets patterns of meaning in text [ 1]. In legal
research it supports close reading of case law to surface codes, propose themes, and
map arguments [ 2], complementing information extraction of court-established facts
in criminal-court opinions [ 3]. Manual TA is slow and hard to port across corpora and
languages [ 4]. I therefore target a practical metric— time-to-ﬁrst-theme (TTF-Theme)—to
free expert time for curation while retaining approval.
I package the approach explored by Drápal, Westermann, and Šavelka into a frontend-
orchestrated, instruction-responsive workﬂow with explicit human-in-the-loop check-
points and audited, rule-based edits [ 2,5]. The design aligns with prior strands on segmen-
tation, fast similarity search, cross-lingual transfer, and zero-shot legal annotation [ 5,6,7].
Our model-agnostic, multilingual architecture reduces bespoke prompt engineering and
increases reproducibility across jurisdictions.

2. Workﬂow, UI, and Human-in-the-Loop
Overview. A frontend orchestrates TA phases P2 →P3→P3b→P4 with lightweight
checks, explicit checkpoints, and cross-document aggregation to stabilise codebooks and
candidate themes. The pipeline operationalises the Drápal–Westermann–Šavelka approach
in a UI with reversible edits and consistent exports.
Modules. Five modules correspond to TA phases:
1)Data & Theme Explorer (pre-ﬂight): upload a single JSON keyed by case_id ;
preview schema and per-case text; a quality panel ﬂags duplicates, missing ﬁelds,
and token-length outliers.
2)Initial Codes (Phase 2): per-case code pills with Regenerate/Add /Edit ; optional
user-supplied seed codes; adjustable code granularity; quick CSV/HTML exports
and progress tracking.
3)Candidate Themes (Phase 3): cluster-and-label codes across cases; themes stream
progressively with short descriptions and evidence snippets; automatic consolida-
tion with optional user regrouping.
4)Final Themes (Phase 3b): planned merge/split/rename/move operations with
audit-tracked edits; ﬁnalize the theme set.
5)Assign Final Themes (Phase 4): planned application of the ﬁnal theme set across
all cases with thresholds and summaries; export enriched JSON and compact
reports.
User control over AI outputs. Users can shape AI behaviour through a model selector
(options including the GPT-5, Claude, and Gemini families), quick instruction pills and a
free-form instruction box in Phase 2; per-case Regenerate and Add more codes dialogs
accept custom instructions; Phase 3 also exposes the model selector; and an optional
Theme Assistant panel supports conversational requests with provider-dependent toggles
for reasoning effort and verbosity.
The system expects a single JSON object keyed by case identiﬁers. On upload, the
explorer validates the schema and reports issues. Users may begin at any phase and may
bring annotated or synthetic data for earlier steps (for example, jumping directly to P3
with an existing codebook). As of October 2025, the prototype is operational through
P3; P3b–P4 and ﬁner UI controls are scheduled for JURIX. Looking ahead, an agentic
controller will run phases independently, iterate on subsets, edit speciﬁc codes or themes
under constraints, and execute analyses over the JSON while reusing the same action
schema and audit trail.
3. Conclusion and Artifact A vailability
I package TA for legal research as an instruction-responsive, end-to-end workﬂow with
checkpoints, audited edits, and traceable exports. The system lowers time-to-ﬁrst-theme
while preserving methodological control and portability across jurisdictions and languages.

Plans and Diversions EA
Galileo SARTORa,1, Guido GOVERNATORIb, Giuseppe PISANOc,
Antonino ROTOLOc, and Adam WYNERa
aSwansea University, United Kingdom
bCentral Queensland University, Australia
cUniversity of Bologna, Italy
Abstract. Autonomous vehicles (AVs) must abide by the Highway Code. An AV
agent would make plans which incorporate legal reasoning. Such plans must ac-
count for contingencies wherein the agent chooses between following a current planthat would lead to a violation of the law or providing an alternative plan whichwould not lead to a violation - a diversion. The paper utilises Defeasible DeonticLogic representing norms and encoded in Answer Set Programming (ASP) whichis integrated with planning in ASP. The paper introduces diversions to address con-tingencies with respect to legal reasoning.
Keywords. defeasible deontic logic, answer set programming, planning, autonomous
vehicles
1. Introduction
Planning is critical in many domains in order to attain goals. However, contingencies may
arise, leading to changes in plans. We refer to such variant plans as diversions. Planning
in a legal setting introduces legal norms – obligations, prohibitions, or permissions – onactions along with sanctions and reparations where the norms are violated. An agent’splan and behaviour may vary depending on its disposition towards legal risk or penalty.
The research focuses on plans of autonomous vehicles (AVs) which have to abide by the
Highway Code
2.
Taking a logic-based approach, the research builds on an encoding of Defeasible
Deontic Logic (DDL), which represents and reasons with legal knowledge, in AnswerSet Programming [1], and utilising ASP planners – DDL-ASP planner. The contribution
enables the DDL-ASP planner to reason with contingencies and propose diversions. Theresearch is scoped: one type of legal signal - the stoplight; one prohibition (on crossing ared light); dispositions of agens legalis and agens economicus; no reasoning behind the
type of agent; limited cost/beneﬁt analysis; a small environment; and no mitigations. Thesystem is the basis for future work.
2. Defeasible Deontic Logic, ASP, and Planning
Defeasible Deontic Logic (DDL) is an eﬃcient rule-based, non-monotonic formalism for
legal reasoning [2]. It combines features of Defeasible Logic for the natural and eﬃcient
