modelling of exceptions with deontic logic, including deontic operators (obligation and
permission), and the ability to reason with violations and compensatory obligations. An-swer Set Programming (ASP) has been established as a powerful formalism for declarativeproblem-solving [3]. DDL has been encoded in ASP [1]. And ASP has long incorporatedplanning [4]. The reader is referred to the literature for technical details.
3. Autonomous Vehicles
The complexity of autonomous driving motivates a hierarchical planning architecture
which distinguishes between global, strategic route selection and local, context-awaredecision making [5, 6]. A global planner cannot account for contingencies, e.g., status
of traﬃc lights, other road users, etc.; a local planner has no strategic reasoning [7].Planning in AVs is generally limited to trajectory prediction [8, 9]. There are diﬀerent
logic-based representations of traﬃc rules, e.g., as BDI models [10, 11] or controlled
natural languages [12].
In this context the global and local planner share the basic world model, diﬀering
in their access to the dynamic components, operating respectively under uncertainty(optimizing the plan by estimated time) and with access to the perceived state (optimizingalso by norm compliance). The dynamic information is included in the ASP theory forthe local planner before the grounding phase. This includes: the updated position, thecurrent direction, the window size, the goal, and any mitigating circumstances such asbeing in an emergency.
We use the ASP optimization mechanisms so the local planner can optimize in
diﬀerent ways, depending on the explicit optimization criteria: minimising the numberof violations; minimising the time to reach the goal; or some combination. In the Pythoncode, the optimization is set when calling the local planner. While in the current statethe reasoning with violations and optimisation is limited. In future developments, thereasoning will be made more context dependent.
The agent operates under a set of norms that regulate its behaviour[13]. A prescriptive
rule obligates the agent to stop at red traﬃc lights, with a monetary ﬁne in cases of non-compliance. A constitutive rule identiﬁes the conditions under which we have a failureto stop, namely, when the agent is obligated to stop yet acts. Exceptions are modelledusing a permissive rule that allows the agent to disregard red lights during emergencysituations. In the short planner, where the execution of an action in a state were to leadto a violation, we say that the plan contains a violation. In such a case, a new long termplan may be calculated.
The environment is modelled as a directed graph consisting of nodes, some of which
contain traﬃc lights. The agent can move between adjacent nodes, with actions modelledin terms of pre- and post-conditions, or stop in the current node. Where the action istaken, the agent’s new position and direction are updated.
If the local plan is compliant (i.e., no violation would occur), it is executed, and the
local plan is called on the next state. Otherwise, the global planner is invoked to ﬁndalternative paths to the global goal.
The analysis illustrates the beneﬁts, in terms of simplicity and consistency, of a shared
DDL-ASP logical representation which integrates the environment, actions, planning,and with reasoning about norms.G. Sartor et al. / Plans and Diversions EA 434

Abstract. Automated decision-making in administrative law holds the promise of
considerable efﬁciency gains, enhanced consistency, and increased transparency.
This extended abstract distills a qualitative study based on semi-structured expertinterviews that adopts a grounded theory approach to investigate the preconditions,constraints, and opportunities for embedding the concept of Digital Twin of Ad-ministrative Law (DTAL) into legislative and administrative processes while safe-guarding the Rule of Law.
Keywords. Legal Ontologies, Semantic Interoperability, Ontological Alignment,

1. Introduction and Methodology
Public administrations worldwide are increasingly exploring automated decision-making
(ADM) systems to improve the efﬁciency and consistency of administrative processessuch as taxation, social beneﬁt determinations, permitting, and enforcement. How-ever, deploying sub-symbolic aritiﬁcal intelligence, e.g., models trained using machine-learning algorithms, in public decision-making raises signiﬁcant concerns regarding theRule of Law, i.e., the principle that governance should occur through publicly disclosed,consistent, and impartial laws. The legal stakes are high, as poorly designed algorithmscan undermine due process, transparency, and equality before the law [3].
Today, agencies and implementers often re-code identical provisions, producing du-
plication, inconsistent outcomes, and fragile maintenance when parameters change [10].A potential solution would be to publish digital twins of legislation: authoritative,
machine-readable counterparts to legal texts that serve as a single source of truth forcomputations and explanations [6, 8, 7]. Previous work [13, 12, 14] outlines the vision ofintegrating legal ontologies with digital twin technology in administrative law, proposingthe promulgation of legislation together with a machine-readable, logically-founded rep-resentation. Building on the broader concept of digital twins from engineering [5, 15],Legal Knowledge and Information Systems

This extended abstract summarizes the results of a qualitative study (see [4] for fur-

2. Discussion and Conclusions
By analyzing the experts’ narratives, we derived key themes that shed light on both the
limitations of automating law and the preconditions for success in that endeavor. Ourﬁndings identify four critical success factors for enabling ADM: (1) embracing only par-tial transformation, acknowledging that not all decisions in law can be automated; (2)achieving semantic standardization and ontological alignment; (3) Transforming legis-lation into high-quality ADM supporting structures; and (4) adapting drafting processesfor legislation and governance mechanisms to accommodate ADM. The results indicatethat partial automation is feasible, particularly in deterministic domains such as taxationand subsidies but legal frameworks require hybrid models that allow for human judgmentand interpretative ﬂexibility.
The ﬁndings support the conceptual design of the concept of a Digital Twin for
Administrative Law (DTAL). Drawing on methods used in industry for digital twins [2]
as well as on the concept of blockchain-based smart contracts [9, 1], this research positsa four-layer structure for a digital twin for administrative law:
1.Statutory T ext: the natural-language law as traditionally published.
2.Ontology: a formal structure encapsulating the law’s semantics.
3.Conﬁguration Model: adjustable parameters which would include the typicalaxioms of the ontology (e.g., tax rates, exemption thresholds).
4.Executable Logic: the computational rules for enforcement (e.g., formulae, con-ditionals).
The ﬁndings of this study are based on a small European sample. Futurer work will
broaden the scope with cross-jurisdictional studies. Future work will also investigate ap-plication of the DTAL concept in other domains and formalize digital-readiness criteriafor legislative pipelines.
Grounded in empirical evidence, our study investigates how the DTAL concept sup-
ports explainable ADM that complies with the Rule of Law. These ﬁndings serve to de-velop a blueprint for code-based administration, establishing a foundation for trusted andcitizen-centric digital government. initial experiment on ﬁve briefs for the Acheson Hotel case, and compared the results with
Author 1’s manual identiﬁcation of attacks. We chose Mistral7B because it performs
relation-based argument mining successfully on several non-legal datasets [5]. While alack of annotated data makes meaningful evaluation challenging, we found the output isstill promising.
Our initial attempts support further investigation on combining the strengths of
LLMs and computational argumentation to help non-legal experts analyze U.S. SupremeCourt briefs. We will investigate how to use LLMs to generate the argument models au-tomatically and use formal semantics, such as ASPIC+ [6], to interpret the briefs further.H.
